[Cloudflare's engineering account](https://blog.cloudflare.com/emudhra-certificate-compromise/) reinforces the operational distinction: its products needed their own updates, and a successful browser or curl check does not certify another application's verifier. Treat that as a test-design lesson. Start at the outbound operation the application actually performs, then follow its HTTP transport, TLS configuration, execution environment and deployed binary. Do not substitute a convenient test from a different application.

For an example review, draw three boxes: the browser you use to inspect a dashboard, the Go service behind that dashboard, and the service's outbound dependency. Place the certificate-verification decision on each connection separately. This small drawing prevents a surprisingly common incident mistake: declaring the whole environment repaired because the most visible client received an update.

sections.title: A certificate chain is a delegated decision, not a green decoration
sections.body:
A service certificate is normally evaluated as part of a path toward a trust anchor. A useful review asks who is permitted to issue the certificate, whether the requested name matches, and whether the verification policy accepts the resulting path. The [crypto/x509 reference](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) documents the verification APIs and their platform-dependent behavior. A parser successfully reading a certificate is not equivalent to successful certificate verification.

For the incident exercise, use the idea of delegation. A leaf certificate is the claimed identity presented at the door; an intermediate supplies authority for that claim. When an intermediate's private key cannot be trusted, checking the leaf's spelling or expiry alone does not repair the delegation. The decision must reject the unsafe authority as well. That explanation is more useful in a code review than an undifferentiated instruction to 'refresh SSL'.

Keep the example conceptual. You do not need recovered private keys, a forged public-site certificate or a demonstration against an external target to learn the failure mode. Controlled local certificates are sufficient to test whether your own transport preserves ordinary verification. Incident-specific protection should additionally be tied to the vendor's fixed release and the artifact you deploy.

sections.title: Inventory the executable that is actually running
sections.body:
Begin an incident worksheet with one row per executable, not one row per repository. Include long-running services, administrative CLIs, worker processes and jobs that run only at night. Record the owner, artifact identity, deployment location, outbound dependencies and evidence location. Leave unknown cells visibly unknown. A tidy spreadsheet full of assumed versions is less useful than an incomplete inventory with named owners.

On a native development or operations machine, inspect an available Go executable using the tool's build-information view:

```bash
go version
go version -m ./bin/service
```

The first command describes the tool you are invoking. The second inspects the named file. They answer different questions. Record both outputs, together with the artifact digest from your existing release system. If the production image is minimal and has no Go command, inspect an exported copy of its executable in the build or incident environment; do not install debugging tools into every running container just to make the worksheet look complete.

Also inspect the startup configuration. A new executable stored beside an old one is not proof that the process manager selected it. Check the path, container image digest or release identifier used by the workload. Give every row a closure condition: for example, 'new digest observed on all active replicas and scheduled-job template updated'.

sections.title: Pin the rebuild inputs and keep the change reviewable
sections.body:
For this incident, the official release history records the fixed patch versions. Check the [current supported release history](https://go.dev/doc/devel/release) before doing operational work; a historical article should never become a permanent instruction to stay on an old patch. Use an exact approved toolchain in the incident build and record what your build system actually selected.

A small native-machine workflow can make that selection explicit:

```bash
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3 go version
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3 go test ./...
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3 go build -trimpath -o ./bin/service ./cmd/service
go version -m ./bin/service
```

These commands illustrate the incident's patched version; substitute a later supported fixed version when appropriate. An exact toolchain may need to be downloaded before an isolated build environment can use it. That is a build-input preparation step, not a promise that a bare offline machine can fetch missing tools.

Keep source changes minimal unless testing reveals a separate defect. Avoid combining a trust repair with a serializer migration, a database-driver upgrade and a wholesale module reorganization. The narrower change is easier to validate and, if an unrelated regression appears, easier to reason about. Our [reproducible-build guide](/news/go-reproducible-build-report-october-21-2026) explains a complementary evidence trail; reproducibility alone is not a vulnerability verdict.

sections.title: Preserve verification while diagnosing TLS failures
sections.body:
A failing connection can create pressure to disable checks 'just temporarily'. That changes the security property you are trying to restore. The [crypto/tls documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls#Config) explains that `InsecureSkipVerify` disables ordinary certificate-chain and hostname verification unless appropriate custom verification replaces it. A successful request made after that change is not evidence that the trust problem was fixed.

Review production transports for verification overrides, custom root pools and callbacks. Treat each as a configuration contract with an owner and tests. A private development CA can be legitimate; a broad bypass added during troubleshooting should not quietly become a production default. Verify proxy and service-mesh boundaries too: decide which component terminates TLS and which component initiates the next protected connection.

Separate error classes in operational notes. An expired certificate, unknown authority, hostname mismatch, refused TCP connection and request deadline are different observations. Recording only 'HTTPS failed' makes teams repeat experiments and encourages inappropriate workarounds. Conversely, avoid writing credentials, private keys or full sensitive URLs into incident logs. The evidence should help another engineer reproduce the configuration decision without disclosing the traffic being protected.

sections.title: Write a local negative-control test before touching production
Scan the source and the resulting binary as separate evidence
sections.body:
Run your existing vulnerability checks on the source tree and on the artifact you intend to deploy. The official [govulncheck command documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck) supports source analysis and binary mode, with different visibility and limitations. Keep those reports distinct rather than treating one as a substitute for the other.

```bash
govulncheck ./...
govulncheck -mode=binary ./bin/service
```

Install a reviewed scanner version in the build environment and record its version, database check time and command. These scans may require network access to obtain vulnerability information; they are not an offline guarantee. Source analysis can provide call-path information that binary analysis cannot reconstruct. A binary report can also include code whose actual runtime reachability needs further investigation.

Our recommended evidence bundle contains the inspected artifact's build information, digest, test result and scanner report. It should name what was checked and what remains uncertain. A clean report does not prove correct authorization, safe retry behavior or the absence of every application vulnerability. A finding is a reason to investigate and repair, not a license to claim exploitation occurred. That distinction keeps incident communication useful to developers and understandable to the people operating the service.

sections.title: Roll out by artifact identity and verify every execution path
sections.body:
Choose a rollout unit that matches the service's failure domain. A canary might be a small replica subset, a staging worker queue or one representative internal job. Before increasing traffic, exercise the outbound dependencies that matter and inspect certificate errors, request success, timeouts and ordinary application health. Compare against a recorded baseline rather than relying on a screenshot of one green endpoint.

Use the deployment system you already operate. For a Kubernetes deployment, for example, the inspected replacement image should be identified by its digest in the reviewed manifest. Track rollout completion and inspect the image identifiers reported by active Pods. [Kubernetes' Deployment documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) describes rollout behavior; it does not make an application's readiness probe certify every outbound TLS path.

Do not forget execution paths outside the main Deployment. CronJobs, migration tools, init containers and administrative binaries can retain older artifacts. A release should not be marked complete merely because the busiest web replicas moved first. Make a separate decision about old job histories and retained images according to your recovery policy; preserving evidence and preventing accidental reuse are related but different responsibilities.

sections.title: Design rollback without silently restoring the vulnerable artifact
sections.body:
A rollback button is valuable, but its meaning deserves a review during a security incident. Rolling back unrelated source behavior may be necessary. Rolling back to an earlier executable can also restore the trust decision you were trying to remove. Prepare a recovery artifact that uses the fixed toolchain while retaining the previous application behavior, then validate it through the same basic tests.

In the release note, name the recovery artifact and its scope. Explain whether it changes application code, configuration or only the compiler/runtime inputs. This is our recommended operational policy, not a guarantee supplied by a Go version number. Teams differ in deployment constraints, and emergency changes still need an accountable owner.

Keep retries bounded while investigating connection failures. An unhealthy certificate path should not trigger an unlimited retry storm or a growing backlog of work. Define a deadline, a finite queue and an explicit failure state. Our [backpressure article](/news/go-backpressure-concurrency-limits-queues-deadlines) provides worked examples of admission and cancellation. Authentication and transport repair do not remove the need for those capacity controls; both properties matter when an incident changes failure rates across many clients at once.

sections.title: Prepare a response drill, not a collection of emergency commands
sections.body:
The Go [security policy](https://go.dev/doc/security/policy) distinguishes PUBLIC, PRIVATE and URGENT tracks. URGENT issues can lead to an immediate dedicated release without the usual preparation window. For application teams, the practical consequence is a need for a rehearsed short path from a trusted advisory to a reviewed replacement artifact.

A useful drill assigns four roles: someone confirms the advisory and affected components; someone builds the replacement; someone checks the evidence; and someone verifies rollout completion. A small team can combine roles, but should still preserve the separate questions. Ask the reviewer to locate the running binary from the worksheet without asking the build author which directory to inspect. Ask the operator to demonstrate that scheduled workloads use the same approved artifact policy as web replicas.

Record the slowest handoff. It may be an abandoned service without an owner, an unavailable builder, missing artifact provenance or a job template that nobody includes in release checks. Improving that bottleneck is often more valuable than writing a longer incident checklist. Retrospectives should produce a concrete change in the normal release process, with a small testable outcome and a named maintainer.

sections.title: Connect the exercise to Go learning and interview preparation
sections.body:
For interviews, explain the boundaries rather than memorizing the incident's dates. Be ready to distinguish parsing from verification, a trust anchor from an intermediate, a browser update from a service rebuild, and a scanner finding from proven exploitability. Then show how a local negative-control test and an artifact inventory answer different questions. That is a stronger demonstration of Go engineering judgment than reciting TLS field names.

Start with [TLS trust](/learn/security.tls-trust), [pinned toolchains](/learn/modules.tools-toolchain), [vulnerability checks](/learn/modules.fuzz-vulnerability) and [Kubernetes rollouts](/learn/operations.kubernetes-rollout). Use the [Go course](/learn?direction=tooling) for the surrounding service-security and deployment concepts, and the [interview library](/interview) to practice explaining the decisions aloud. Read the [app guide](/guide) before choosing an execution environment: GopherForge's bundled Go/WASI sandbox has no guest networking. The TLS server example and deployment commands in this article belong in a native Go environment; a Playground's shared Output does not establish that another participant ran a production test.

The final worksheet should tell a short, checkable story: this was the artifact, this was the verification path, these inputs produced its replacement, these tests ran, and these workloads now use it. Publish conclusions at the strength of that evidence. Keep the rest as an explicit follow-up, so the next urgent update starts with a maintained system instead of a fresh search through forgotten binaries.

title: Go database/sql under load: pools, timeouts and transactions
description: Diagnose Go SQL pool waits, release Rows, budget connections across replicas, and design transactions, deadlines and retries with worked PostgreSQL examples.

sections.title: When a fast database still produces a slow API
sections.body:
A Go API can time out while its database reports short query durations. The missing time may be spent before the query begins: waiting for a connection, waiting for an application admission slot, or waiting behind work that nobody still needs. Increasing the connection limit treats all three situations as though the database had spare capacity. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the change merely moves the queue into PostgreSQL, makes more transactions compete for the same rows, and increases the cost of every request.

Consider a fictional order service. Its ordinary query takes eight milliseconds in a quiet staging environment, but its production endpoint occasionally takes two seconds. That comparison proves little by itself. Staging might have different data, fewer locks, warmer caches, or no competing reports. The useful investigation follows one request through its actual lifetime: admission, connection acquisition, query execution, result consumption and response writing. A duration measured around the whole repository method includes several of those stages; a database execution statistic may include only one.

This guide builds a concrete operating model for database/sql. The numbers are illustrative budgets, not benchmark results or recommended defaults. The aim is to make capacity and ownership explicit enough that an incident can be explained, reproduced and repaired. Start with the course readings on [pool lifetime](/learn/sql.pool-lifetime) and [rows and cancellation](/learn/sql.rows-and-context) if the API is unfamiliar.

sections.title: Budget connections across the entire deployment
sections.body:
A pool belongs to an application process. The database serves the sum of all processes, plus migrations, administration, reporting jobs and other applications. Therefore a per-process setting cannot be evaluated without the maximum number of simultaneous processes. Include rolling-update surge, autoscaling, old replicas that are still draining, and separate worker deployments that use their own pools.

Suppose a database capacity review allocates this application a ceiling of 120 connections. Six ordinary replicas plus two surge replicas, each capped at twelve, can consume 96. Four migration connections and ten reserved for operations bring the planned total to 110, leaving ten as headroom. That is an arithmetic exercise, not evidence that this database should run 110 active queries. Its useful concurrency might be lower because CPU, storage or lock contention becomes limiting first.

Idle connections count inside the open-connection limit; they are not an extra allowance. Likewise, a transaction holding one connection is already part of that process's total. Keep a simple capacity worksheet with the peak replica count, process roles, pool caps and operational reserve. Review it when changing deployment strategy, not just when touching database code.

The official [connection-management guide](https://go.dev/doc/database/manage-connections) explains the pool controls. The engineering decision is how those controls fit your system. A pool cap limits connections, while a separate admission policy limits how much work the service is willing to queue before reaching that pool. Our [backpressure guide](/news/go-backpressure-concurrency-limits-queues-deadlines) develops that second boundary.

sections.title: Configure deliberately, then look for evidence
sections.body:
Create one long-lived database handle for a database role and share it between repository operations. Opening a new handle for every request multiplies independent pools and defeats the intended cap. Opening a handle is also different from proving that authentication and connectivity work; perform a bounded readiness check during startup when your availability policy requires it.

```go
func configurePool(db *sql.DB) {
    // Illustrative values: derive these from deployment and DB budgets.
    db.SetMaxOpenConns(12)
    db.SetMaxIdleConns(6)
    db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(2 * time.Minute)
    db.SetConnMaxLifetime(20 * time.Minute)
}
```

Lifetime settings encourage replacement of old connections; they are not a per-query timeout or a promise that a busy connection is interrupted at an exact age. Choose them with knowledge of proxies, server-side idle limits and connection-establishment cost. If reconnects become frequent, investigate the mismatch rather than continually shortening the lifetime.

Document why each setting exists and what would make you change it. For example, a lower idle limit may release expensive idle sessions during quiet periods, while an excessively low limit can create avoidable reconnect churn during bursts. A configuration review should include both a busy period and a quiet-to-busy transition. The correct setting is the one supported by representative observations, not the largest value that avoids an error in a synthetic loop.

sections.title: Treat result rows as a resource with an owner
Give waiting and execution one deadline budget
sections.body:
A request deadline should cover the work the user actually waits for. If a request spends most of its budget waiting for a connection, granting the eventual query a fresh full timeout can extend the operation far beyond that expectation. Propagate the request context, then derive a shorter child deadline only when the database operation deserves a stricter local limit.

The Go guide to [cancelling database operations](https://go.dev/doc/database/cancel-operations) demonstrates context-aware calls. Actual interruption also depends on driver and server behavior. Verify the selected driver against the database you deploy. A context error tells you that a caller's budget ended; it does not independently establish whether a remote write committed.

Always call the cancellation function returned by WithTimeout. Distinguish cancellation by the client, an internal deadline and a database failure in metrics, while returning an appropriate public response without leaking connection strings or SQL parameters. Preserve the causal error for diagnostic code rather than turning every failure into an unstructured message.

An especially revealing test occupies the only permitted connection, starts a second context-aware operation, cancels that operation, and checks that it returns without increasing the pool size. This tests waiting behavior separately from query cancellation. It does not certify the database server's cancellation implementation; that requires an integration test with the real driver and server.

sections.title: A transaction must keep all its database work inside
Separate isolation requirements from connection problems
sections.body:
A pool can be healthy while transactions block each other on the database. Increasing pool size then gives more transactions permission to wait on the same contended resource. Inspect the database's activity and wait information alongside application measurements. Ask whether a long-running transaction, an inconsistent lock order or a missing index explains the symptom.

Isolation is a correctness decision. Write down the invariant in a sentence before choosing a level: for example, one inventory unit must not be reserved twice, or a transfer must preserve a defined total. Then identify how the schema, statements, constraints and isolation enforce it under concurrency. A preliminary read followed by an unrelated update is not automatically safe because both statements use a transaction.

PostgreSQL's [isolation documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) describes when transactions can be rejected and require another attempt. The response should restart the complete transaction when that is the documented recovery path, not repeat an arbitrary final statement against an aborted transaction.

Also shorten the time between the first statement and commit. Preparing a large response, waiting for a human decision or fetching a remote document inside that interval makes connection ownership and lock duration depend on unrelated systems. Moving that work outside the transaction can be a larger improvement than any pool-setting adjustment. Preserve correctness while changing the boundary; a shorter transaction that loses the invariant is not an improvement.

sections.title: Retry an understood outcome, not every error
sections.body:
Retries consume the same scarce connections and execution budget as original attempts. A service that retries three times during a database incident can multiply pressure while telling its caller that it is being resilient. Classify failures using the real driver's error types and database error codes, apply a bounded retry policy only to supported cases, and stop when the parent context is done.

Keep the transaction retry unit separate from externally visible side effects. If an attempt sends an email and then encounters a retryable database failure, a complete retry can send another email. A durable outbox, an idempotency key or an explicitly recoverable workflow may be appropriate, depending on the business action. None is supplied automatically by database/sql.

A commit error deserves special attention. A broken connection while waiting for commit acknowledgement may leave the client uncertain about the remote outcome. Treating every such error as proof that nothing happened is unsafe. Design a way to look up an operation by its stable business identifier before deciding to submit it again.

Read [retry and idempotency](/learn/sql.retry-and-idempotency) together with [isolation and locks](/learn/sql.isolation-and-locks). A useful review exercise is to list each side effect, the point where it becomes durable, and the evidence available after a timeout. That table usually exposes ambiguous states more clearly than a generic retry helper.

sections.title: Measure connection pressure separately from query latency
sections.body:
DB.Stats exposes process-local pool observations. Export the open, in-use and idle counts as gauges. Treat WaitCount and WaitDuration as cumulative values, and calculate changes over the same observation interval. Dividing the change in wait duration by the change in wait count gives an average for waits that were recorded in that interval; it is not a latency percentile and does not describe every request.

Correlate those measurements with arrival rate, completed operations, deadline failures, replica count, transaction duration and database wait events. A rising wait count with consistently saturated in-use connections suggests one investigation. A large idle pool alongside high database execution latency suggests another. Neither proves the final cause without tracing or a controlled reproduction.

The database's own [activity statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/monitoring-stats.html) help distinguish active execution, blocked sessions and transactions left open. Keep diagnostics accessible during an outage by preserving the operational connection reserve. Avoid exporting SQL parameter values, raw customer identifiers or unbounded query strings as metric labels.

Create one incident dashboard that shows the whole path. Otherwise the API team may show a timeout chart while the database team shows a fast-query chart, and both charts can be accurate. The purpose of instrumentation is to reconcile those observations into one explanation, not to choose which team appears correct.

sections.title: Reproduce the failure you actually care about
sections.body:
A useful test matrix changes one pressure source at a time. Begin with a steady load, then add a short burst. Repeat with a deliberately slow query, a held transaction, an early-abandoned result and a cancelled caller. Finally exercise a rolling deployment so that old and new processes briefly share the database budget. Record the exact schema, dataset scale, driver version and configuration.

Measure useful completions and failures as well as response latency. A system can make a percentile look better by rejecting most requests, or make success rate look better by letting a queue grow until memory becomes the failure mechanism. State the service objective and the acceptable rejection policy before comparing configurations.

For cancellation and rollback tests, verify database state after the request returns. For lock tests, use barriers or explicit transactions to establish the intended ordering rather than hoping that two concurrent clients overlap. For pool-wait tests, a small synthetic driver can validate local ownership behavior, but it cannot replace a PostgreSQL integration environment.

Run these exercises against disposable data. A load generator aimed at production without an agreed budget can create the very incident it is meant to investigate. The examples accompanying this article are small local regression checks, not a measured capacity recommendation for your deployment.

sections.title: Turn the investigation into a maintainable contract
sections.body:
The final artifact should be more useful than a larger number in a configuration file. Keep the capacity worksheet, one bounded result-reading example, the transaction owner, cancellation expectations, retry classification and a reproducible test scenario beside the service. Give every resource a documented owner and every queue a reason to exist.

When reviewing a change, ask what happens during a rollout, when the caller leaves, when a result is abandoned and when a commit acknowledgement disappears. These questions connect code structure to operational behavior. They also make strong interview preparation because they require explaining a concrete invariant rather than reciting pool method names.

Continue with [SQL interview scenarios](/interview/http.sql), [bounded concurrency](/learn/concurrency.bounded-work) and [HTTP connection ownership](/news/go-1-27-http-connection-reuse). The same discipline appears in all three: define a budget, acquire deliberately, release reliably, and measure where time was spent. A well-tuned pool is one part of that contract. It cannot compensate for an unbounded queue, a leaked result or an undefined retry outcome.

[Download the original compilable examples and tests](/downloads/go-engineering-examples-20261029.zip). The ZIP includes imports, the local regression suite and a README explaining exactly what was verified.

title: Go graceful shutdown: HTTP, workers and Kubernetes
description: Build a Go HTTP shutdown lifecycle with readiness, one grace budget, worker ownership and draining. Includes code, Kubernetes YAML and a practical test plan.

sections.title: A rollout is part of normal service behavior
sections.body:
A Go service that passes its request tests can still lose work whenever a deployment replaces it. The failure often appears as a small burst of connection resets, abandoned jobs or duplicate writes. Because the burst is brief, teams sometimes accept it as an unavoidable property of Kubernetes. A better starting point is to treat shutdown as an ordinary lifecycle transition with explicit ownership, deadlines and observable outcomes.

Imagine an API that creates export jobs. During a rollout, one replica receives a termination signal while it is accepting requests, writing job records and streaming an existing download. Those activities have different completion conditions. A request may finish when its response is written; a durable job may continue on another worker; a stream may require its own protocol for reconnecting. One call to Server.Shutdown cannot decide the business policy for all of them.

This guide assembles a practical shutdown design, including a minimal HTTP example and a test plan. The time budgets are examples for reasoning, not claims about network propagation or a universal Kubernetes configuration. Start with [HTTP service lifecycle](/learn/services.http-lifecycle) and [probes and shutdown](/learn/operations.probes-and-shutdown) for the underlying APIs. The important outcome is a service that can explain which work it accepts, which work it finishes, and which work it deliberately abandons when its deadline expires.

sections.title: Separate admission, draining, cancellation and completion
sections.body:
These four actions are related but different. Admission determines whether new work may enter. Draining allows already accepted work to finish. Cancellation asks selected work to stop. Completion establishes that the owner has actually observed its children exit. A service that cancels everything immediately may not drain anything. A service that merely requests cancellation may exit before cleanup happens.

Write a resource table before writing lifecycle code. For each HTTP listener, queue consumer, scheduler, database pool, outbound transport and long-lived session, identify the owner, the stop-accepting action, the completion signal and the deadline. Shared dependencies must remain available until their last legitimate user has finished.

For the fictional export service, the HTTP listener stops new requests, a queue consumer stops fetching new jobs, and an active export either completes within a defined allowance or records recoverable progress. The database stays available while accepted handlers and workers persist their final state. Closing the pool first turns an orderly exit into a cascade of artificial database errors.

This ordering is an application design recommendation, not a guarantee supplied by the platform. A request may have already crossed a proxy while a readiness update is propagating. An unexpected process crash provides no graceful window at all. Correctness must therefore also survive interruption, using durable state and idempotent operations where the business action requires them.

sections.title: The Kubernetes grace period is a shared budget
sections.body:
The Kubernetes [Pod lifecycle documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/) describes a termination grace period, termination signals and eventual forced termination. A configured preStop hook consumes time within that lifecycle; it is not a free extra interval added before the application's allowance begins.

Suppose the chosen Pod grace period is forty seconds. A team might budget five seconds for measured routing preparation, twenty-five for request draining, five for worker completion and five for cleanup and scheduling uncertainty. The sum matters. If each component independently allocates the full forty seconds, the composed lifecycle cannot fit inside forty seconds.

Use one absolute shutdown deadline when coordinating several components. Derive child deadlines from the remaining time or explicitly reserve time for later cleanup. A chain of fresh thirty-second timeouts is not a thirty-second shutdown. It is potentially several minutes of shutdown that the orchestrator may interrupt much earlier.

Do not build correctness around the grace period always being available. Node failure, resource exhaustion and an administrative force deletion can bypass the intended path. A grace period improves the probability of an orderly transition; it is not a transactional boundary. Record unfinished durable work so another owner can recover it, and test the recovery path separately from the graceful path.

sections.title: Readiness changes routing intent, not reality instantly
sections.body:
Readiness answers whether a replica should receive normal traffic. Liveness answers whether restarting the process may help. Startup probes protect slow initialization from premature liveness failures. Their roles should remain distinct; a temporary database outage should not automatically cause every otherwise healthy API process to restart simultaneously.

The official [probe guide](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) explains these mechanics. For shutdown, make readiness reflect the transition toward draining. Keep liveness meaningful while the process is still executing its shutdown responsibilities, rather than declaring it dead simply because it has stopped accepting new work.

EndpointSlice updates and data-plane behavior are separate layers. Kubernetes exposes readiness and termination information, but your ingress, load balancer, service mesh and existing connections determine how traffic actually reaches a process. The [EndpointSlice reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices/) is useful for understanding those conditions; it does not establish a fixed propagation delay for every cluster.

Measure that delay in the environment you operate. If a preparation interval is needed, include it inside the total budget and explain what evidence supports its duration. An unexplained sleep copied from another team's YAML can spend most of a small grace period without establishing that any relevant routing component has stopped sending traffic.

sections.title: Use a fresh context for the drain operation
sections.body:
A common shutdown bug passes the already-cancelled signal context to Server.Shutdown. The application receives a termination signal, cancels its lifecycle context, and immediately tells Shutdown that its own deadline is over. The resulting forced closure then looks like a failure of graceful shutdown rather than a context-ownership mistake.

Use the signal context to trigger the transition. Create a separate bounded context for the drain. Keep request contexts alive while they are intentionally allowed to finish, unless your policy explicitly cancels them. If Server.BaseContext is derived directly from the signal context, cancellation may reach every handler at the first signal, defeating that policy.

Signal handling also needs an owner. The standard [os/signal reference](https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#NotifyContext) describes NotifyContext and its stop function. Releasing the notification registration after the first signal can restore ordinary behavior for a subsequent interrupt when the process otherwise has the default disposition. Verify the actual process tree and container entrypoint instead of assuming a shell forwards signals correctly.

Keep cleanup functions bounded and error-aware. Log a drain timeout as an incomplete shutdown, not as a successful deployment event. If force-closing ordinary HTTP connections is the chosen fallback, make that explicit and ensure callers have an idempotent recovery path for ambiguous writes.

sections.title: A minimal HTTP owner that waits for shutdown
Join workers before closing their dependencies
sections.body:
Background work needs a completion signal just as request-serving work does. For a queue consumer, distinguish stopping new fetches from cancelling an already running job. For a periodic scheduler, stop creating new tasks before waiting for the tasks it already created. A WaitGroup can count completions, but it does not define cancellation, persistence or retry policy.

A useful lifecycle interface might expose StopAccepting, Drain and Close, provided those names have documented semantics and do not hide ownership. Simpler services can use explicit functions and channels instead. The abstraction is worthwhile only when it makes the real sequence easier to inspect.

Cancellation should reach every blocking operation a worker owns: queue reads, database calls, outbound requests and sends to result channels. A goroutine stuck sending a final status to an abandoned receiver can prevent completion even though its main job has stopped. If a channel has multiple producers, define who closes it after all producers finish; closing it from an arbitrary worker creates a different shutdown failure.

Use [cancel and join](/learn/concurrency.cancel-and-join) as a review checklist. The most useful question is often simple: after requesting cancellation, which line establishes that this goroutine is gone? If the answer is an arbitrary sleep or the process exit itself, the lifecycle is relying on timing rather than completion evidence.

sections.title: Long-lived protocols need their own drain strategy
sections.body:
Ordinary HTTP request draining is not the same as draining a WebSocket, a hijacked connection, a long-running stream or an independent RPC server. Each protocol can have a different notion of a session, accepted work and reconnect safety. Inventory these paths explicitly, including endpoints that are rarely exercised during a deployment.

For a subscription service, a reasonable policy might stop new subscriptions, notify existing clients of an upcoming disconnect, allow a bounded period to acknowledge or checkpoint, then close remaining sessions. The exact mechanism belongs to that protocol. A list of active sessions must itself have a concurrency-safe owner and a completion signal; a notification callback alone is not proof that all sessions have exited.

For streaming downloads, consider whether clients can resume safely and whether keeping the process alive for an arbitrarily large transfer is acceptable. For durable jobs, distinguish an in-process stream from the durable job state so that a new replica can recover the latter. Clients should not have to infer completion from a connection closing at an unknown point.

Document what the shutdown deadline means for these protocols. If an operation exceeds the allowed window, define the recovery path before relying on a retry. A forced disconnect after a committed write can produce the same ambiguity discussed in our [SQL pool and transaction guide](/news/go-database-sql-pool-timeouts-transactions).

sections.title: Make the deployment configuration match the code
sections.body:
A service whose internal drain limit is twenty-five seconds should not be deployed with a ten-second external grace period. Conversely, a very large grace period can slow recovery when workers never finish. Choose the configuration from measured work duration, routing behavior and a clear maximum recovery delay.

```yaml
# Pod-spec excerpt; image, ports and resources belong in the complete manifest.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.example.com/api:verified-release
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /readyz
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 2
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /livez
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 10
```

This excerpt deliberately omits a preStop hook. Add one only when it performs an understood preparation step and fits inside the shared budget. The [container lifecycle hook documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/) describes the mechanism. Ensure the command or HTTP endpoint actually exists in the image and that administrative drain endpoints are not exposed to untrusted callers.

Also review rolling-update surge and unavailable-replica settings against dependency capacity. Draining old replicas and starting new ones can temporarily increase total database connections. A rollout that preserves HTTP availability but exhausts the shared database budget has moved the outage, not removed it. Tie these settings to the capacity worksheet rather than reviewing application code and manifests independently.

sections.title: Test shutdown with observable barriers
sections.body:
A useful local test starts a real loopback listener, admits a handler that announces it has started, then blocks that handler on a release channel. Cancel the lifecycle context and assert that the lifecycle owner has not returned while the accepted handler is still deliberately blocked. Release it, read the expected response, and confirm that shutdown returns successfully.

A second test deliberately keeps work beyond a short drain deadline and verifies the documented fallback and error. A third checks a startup failure so that the process does not wait forever for a signal after its listener has already failed. Use channels to establish ordering; do not rely on sleeping long enough for a goroutine to probably start.

These tests validate the local HTTP owner. They do not establish ingress propagation time, Pod hook behavior or database recovery. Exercise those separately in a disposable cluster: keep a bounded stream of requests running while performing a rollout, track request identifiers, and compare accepted work with durable outcomes. Include old and new versions if their protocols or schemas differ.

Read the [deterministic concurrency testing guide](/news/go-concurrency-tests-synctest-without-sleeps) for the distinction between coordination evidence and elapsed time. A green local test is valuable precisely because its claim is narrow and reproducible.

sections.title: Observe transitions and define the forced-exit outcome
sections.body:
Record when shutdown begins, when admission stops, when HTTP draining completes, when workers exit and when resources close. Count active work at each boundary. Include a bounded reason such as deployment, operator signal or startup failure. Avoid turning arbitrary request identifiers into metric labels.

The most useful alert is not simply that a Pod terminated. Termination is expected during a rollout. Look for repeated drain deadlines, unfinished durable jobs, client-visible errors and a mismatch between admitted work and acknowledged outcomes. A histogram of shutdown duration helps explain whether a new release changed the lifecycle, but it should be interpreted alongside those outcome measurements.

Finally, practice interruption without a graceful window. A durable job system should recover from a process disappearing, not just from a politely cancelled context. A client retry should not create duplicate business operations because the last response was lost. Graceful shutdown reduces disruption; recovery design handles the failures that do not ask permission.

Continue with [Kubernetes rollout inspection](/learn/operations.kubernetes-rollout), [bounded work](/learn/concurrency.bounded-work) and [service shutdown interview preparation](/interview/http.shutdown). A strong service has a lifecycle that can be described in order, exercised under a deadline and verified through outcomes. That is a more durable result than a shutdown function copied into main without a resource owner.

[Download the original compilable examples and tests](/downloads/go-engineering-examples-20261029.zip). The ZIP includes imports, the local regression suite and a README explaining exactly what was verified.

title: Go concurrency tests: synctest, timers and cancellation
description: Test Go timers and cancellation with testing/synctest, channel barriers, negative controls and race detection. Includes a worked example and layered CI workflow.

sections.title: Replace timing guesses with observable contracts
sections.body:
A concurrent test that occasionally fails in CI is not merely annoying. It makes every failure harder to interpret: a real regression can be dismissed as another scheduling accident, while an arbitrary timeout increase can hide the condition the test was meant to expose. Reliable concurrency tests begin by deciding what must happen before an assertion is allowed to run.

Consider a small delayed notification component. It must not produce a value before a deadline, it must produce one value afterwards, and cancellation before the deadline must stop it without producing a value. Those are three different claims. A test that waits one second and checks a shared boolean may establish none of them, especially when it also accesses that boolean without synchronization.

This guide develops a complete small example using channels and testing/synctest, then separates its guarantees from race detection and integration testing. The examples target the stable Go 1.25-or-later Test API and were checked with a native Go 1.27.3 toolchain. They do not require a live network, database or cloud service. For the app's different execution environment and limits, see the [GopherForge guide](/guide); native desktop verification is not a claim that every operating-system integration runs unchanged inside the app sandbox.

sections.title: Write down the event that makes an assertion legal
sections.body:
Before choosing a test tool, describe the lifecycle in observable terms. When is the worker started? What proves that it has accepted an input? What signals that a result is available? What tells the owner that cancellation has completed? These questions often reveal that the production API itself lacks a useful ownership boundary.

A start channel, a completion channel or a returned result channel can provide concrete evidence. A sleep provides elapsed time, which is different evidence. Even a large delay does not force a heavily loaded machine to schedule a particular goroutine before the test continues. A machine being fast enough yesterday is not part of a concurrency contract.

Keep test instrumentation small and tied to a real boundary. It can be appropriate to inject a narrow dependency that reports an operation starting, but avoid adding a maze of test-only sleeps and global flags throughout production code. Prefer an API whose owner can already observe completion. That makes both the implementation and its tests easier to shut down correctly.

Use the [cancel-and-join lesson](/learn/concurrency.cancel-and-join) to review the owner relationship. A useful exercise is to draw one arrow for starting work and a second arrow for observing its end. If the second arrow has no endpoint, the test may be trying to compensate for a missing lifecycle contract.

sections.title: Understand what a synctest bubble controls
sections.body:
The stable testing/synctest API runs a test function and the goroutines it starts inside an isolated bubble. Time inside that bubble is virtualized. This allows tests to explore timers and deadlines without making the developer wait for equivalent wall-clock durations. It is particularly useful when the behavior of interest is a relationship between time and local asynchronous work.

The official [package reference](https://pkg.go.dev/testing/synctest) defines which operations count as durably blocked and how Wait behaves. Do not replace those rules with the assumption that any blocked goroutine makes the bubble idle. External operating-system activity and goroutines created outside the bubble can change what the test can control.

The Go team's [Testing Time article](https://go.dev/blog/testing-time) explains the design motivation. The practical engineering rule is to keep the component under test self-contained: local goroutines, explicit channels and controlled dependencies. A bubble is not a virtual Kubernetes cluster, a database simulator or an exhaustive model checker for every scheduler interleaving.

Older experimental examples used a different API. Use the stable Test API for this guide, and check the selected toolchain with go version before copying code from an older article. The [Go 1.25 release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.25) document that transition. A version mismatch is a tooling problem to resolve, not a reason to silently rewrite the test's intended contract.

sections.title: Give the delayed operation one owner and one result channel
Test the boundary before and after the deadline
Cancellation must have an observable end
Synchronization is still a production responsibility
sections.body:
Virtual time does not turn unsynchronized application memory into a safe concurrent design. A test that reads a shared map while another goroutine writes it still needs the relevant synchronization boundary. The [Go memory model](https://go.dev/ref/mem) describes the ordering relationships that make concurrent memory access meaningful.

Use channels, mutexes, atomics or ownership according to the data contract. A channel send and receive can transfer a result, while a mutex can protect a collection accessed repeatedly. An atomic flag is useful for one state observation; it does not automatically protect the mutable object the flag points toward. Match the primitive to the invariant instead of adding one wherever the race detector complains.

Within a synctest bubble, Wait supplies documented synchronization for observations after goroutines have durably blocked. That is a testing facility, not a synchronization operation your production caller can invoke. Production APIs still need the necessary boundaries when the helper runs outside the test harness.

Our example communicates entirely through its result channel and context. That makes its ownership inspectable without relying on a test-only shared boolean. For a larger service, apply the same reasoning to every mutable structure, including registries used only during shutdown and caches updated by background refreshers.

sections.title: Keep real I/O in a different test layer
sections.body:
A database query, a DNS lookup or a real socket operation can depend on the operating system, another process and a network. Those dependencies do not become a fully controlled virtual environment because their caller happens to run inside a bubble. Inject a small local substitute when the unit test is about retry timing, scheduling or cancellation decisions.

Keep the interface narrow. A retry component might need a function that returns a result or an error, not an elaborate mock of the entire database driver. Make the substitute report attempts through channels so the test can establish ordering. Supply distinct failures deliberately, including a permanent failure and a context cancellation, rather than making every call succeed after a fixed delay.

Then add integration tests for the real boundary. A loopback HTTP test can verify listener behavior; a disposable database can verify driver cancellation and transaction outcomes; a cluster exercise can verify readiness propagation during rollout. Each layer should state what it controls and what it merely observes.

The standard [httptest package](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest) is useful for HTTP tests, but even a convenient local server remains a different environment from ingress and load-balancer routing. The [graceful shutdown guide](/news/go-http-graceful-shutdown-kubernetes) shows how to combine explicit local barriers with a separate deployment-level test plan.

sections.title: Use negative controls to test the test
sections.body:
A test can be deterministic and still assert the wrong thing. Introduce a small intentional defect, run the relevant test, and confirm that the failure explains the broken contract. Then restore the implementation. This mutation is a local verification technique, not a change to publish in the application.

For the delayed helper, an immediate send should fail the before-deadline assertion. Ignoring cancellation should fail the cancellation case because a notification becomes visible instead of the expected closure. Sending twice should fail the single-result requirement. These are focused negative controls, not a claim that three mutations cover every possible bug.

Look for assertions that survive all of those mutations. A test that checks only that some value eventually arrives may miss both early delivery and duplicate delivery. A test that accepts either a result or a closed channel may not establish cancellation semantics at all. Strengthen the specific contract instead of increasing repetition until a failure appears.

Be careful with intentionally deadlocking mutations. Run them with a bounded test-process timeout and capture the expected failure, so the verification itself does not hang indefinitely. Separate negative-control results from the green suite in your report. A failed mutant test is evidence of detection; a failed unmodified test is an unresolved defect.

sections.title: Add race detection without claiming exhaustive proof
sections.body:
The official [race-detector documentation](https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector) explains that detection depends on code actually executing. A green race run is useful evidence about those executions, not proof that no race exists in an unvisited path. Deterministic timing tests and race detection therefore answer related but different questions.

```sh
go version
go test ./...
go test -race ./...
go test -race -count=100 ./...
go test -shuffle=on ./...
```

Use repetition and shuffling as supplements. They can expose interactions between tests or code paths, but they do not repair an assertion that lacks a completion boundary. Pin the toolchain and record the package set so another engineer can reproduce the result. A race-enabled binary also has different resource costs from an ordinary build; do not treat its throughput as a production benchmark.

For CI, keep fast contract tests close to each change and run the required integration environments at an appropriate stage. Preserve the failure seed or shuffle information when it is available. An intermittent failure becomes easier to investigate when the report includes the exact command, toolchain and observed transition, rather than only a screenshot of a red job.

sections.title: Apply the method to retries, caches and shutdown
sections.body:
The same pattern works beyond timers. For retries, observe each attempt and verify that permanent errors stop the loop. For cache refresh, establish when the new snapshot becomes visible and whether stale readers retain valid ownership. For shutdown, signal that a handler has been admitted, begin draining, and verify that the lifecycle owner waits for its completion.

In each case, distinguish a time boundary from a scheduling boundary. A timer becoming due does not necessarily mean a worker has already published its result. A cancellation function returning does not necessarily mean every child has exited. A cache refresh finishing does not mean a reader stopped using an older snapshot. Make the relevant transition observable before asserting the next state.

These examples are particularly useful in code review because they expose vague API promises. If a reviewer cannot explain which event makes the assertion legal, the implementation may also leave callers guessing about when it is safe to release resources or begin another operation.

Continue with [synctest in the course](/learn/concurrency.synctest), [memory-order interview preparation](/interview/concurrency.memory-order), and [goroutine ownership and leak investigation](/news/go-1-27-goroutine-leak-profiles). Reliable tests do not require pretending concurrency is simple. They require narrowing each claim until its evidence is explicit, its failure is understandable and its dependencies are controlled.

[Download the original compilable examples and tests](/downloads/go-engineering-examples-20261029.zip). The ZIP includes imports, the local regression suite and a README explaining exactly what was verified.

title: Go garbage collection: a practical GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT lab
description: Understand Go garbage collection with tested GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT experiments, live-heap accounting, allocation traffic and a reproducible memory-budget workflow.

sections.title: Start with the symptom, not a collector setting
sections.body:
A Go service with rising memory use does not necessarily have a garbage-collector problem. It may be retaining a larger cache, admitting more concurrent requests, buffering larger payloads, or keeping abandoned work alive. Conversely, a service with a stable live heap can spend substantial CPU repeatedly collecting short-lived allocations. Those incidents require different changes even when the same memory graph appears in both incident reports.

Imagine a document-processing API that reads an input, constructs several temporary representations, and keeps a small result in a cache. After traffic increases, CPU and memory both rise. Before changing GOGC, ask which quantity changed: requests per second, allocated bytes per request, retained bytes per result, concurrent operations, or the size of the cache. A collector cannot decide which cached documents the business no longer needs, and it cannot make an unbounded queue into a bounded one.

This guide combines a short model of Go GC controls with an original, deliberately small experiment. The measurements were made with native Go 1.27.3 on darwin/arm64, Apple M4, with GOMAXPROCS set to two. They are useful for understanding relationships, not choosing production defaults. The complete program, raw observations and commands are downloadable below. The [GC-budget lesson](/learn/runtime.gc-budget) provides a shorter introduction; here we focus on turning observations into a defensible engineering decision.

sections.title: Keep four memory quantities separate
sections.body:
Begin with live heap, allocation traffic, runtime-managed memory and operating-system memory. Live heap describes objects still reachable after collection. Allocation traffic describes memory requested over an interval, including objects that have already become garbage. Runtime-managed memory includes more than the live heap. A process's operating-system footprint also includes memory outside the collector's direct accounting.

These quantities answer different questions. A temporary parser can allocate hundreds of megabytes while retaining almost nothing after a batch finishes. A cache can allocate little during a quiet interval while holding a large existing object graph. A service can release Go objects without immediately showing the same reduction in an operating-system residency chart. A useful dashboard should not label all of those measurements simply as memory.

The [runtime memory-statistics reference](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime#MemStats) defines the individual fields. Keep their names in your measurements so that another engineer can reproduce the interpretation. For example, TotalAlloc is a cumulative counter, while HeapAlloc is a current heap measurement; comparing them as though both described current retained data leads to misleading conclusions.

Our document API should therefore record at least the input size, concurrency, allocation traffic and retained state alongside latency. Without that workload context, a change in the memory chart may reflect a different amount of useful work rather than an improvement or regression in memory management.

sections.title: Use the GOGC model to reason about headroom
sections.body:
The official [Go GC guide](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide) describes a simplified relationship between the live heap, roots and the next heap target. In that model, the target is the live heap plus additional room proportional to the live heap and roots, scaled by GOGC. The model explains a tradeoff; it is not a promise about exact RSS, a fixed allocation size or every point in a concurrent collection cycle.

```text
approximate target = live heap + (live heap + roots) × GOGC / 100
```

A larger GOGC generally permits more allocation headroom between collections. A smaller value generally asks the runtime to collect more frequently. Neither choice changes whether an application still owns a particular object. If the cache permanently retains twice as much useful or useless data, changing the collector percentage does not remove that ownership.

Use the model as a hypothesis generator. If allocation traffic is high but retained state is small, investigate allocation sites. If retained state grows with cache entries, investigate the cache policy. If a workload has many pointer-rich objects, consider the shape and amount of data the collector must inspect, not only total bytes. The companion [heap-graph investigation](/news/go-heap-graphs-reachability-retained-memory) makes that distinction concrete.

sections.title: A memory limit is not a hard process-size guarantee
sections.body:
GOMEMLIMIT and runtime/debug.SetMemoryLimit provide a soft limit for memory managed by the Go runtime. The [SetMemoryLimit documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/debug#SetMemoryLimit) defines its accounting in terms of Sys minus HeapReleased. It also identifies excluded sources such as memory managed outside Go. Therefore setting the runtime limit equal to a container's hard memory allowance does not establish a complete safety margin.

Budget for the whole process and its environment. Depending on the program, that can include native libraries, explicit mappings, binary pages and operating-system overhead. Measure the actual deployment instead of subtracting an arbitrary percentage from a number copied out of a manifest. If the program already needs nearly all available memory for reachable objects, an aggressively low soft limit may increase collection pressure without creating the missing capacity.

Treat the container allowance and runtime control as related but separate decisions. A useful configuration record states the hard environment limit, expected live data, measured non-heap overhead, transient work and operational reserve. It also states what the service does when demand exceeds that budget: reject work, reduce concurrency, evict entries, or move work elsewhere.

Our fictional API might first limit concurrent document conversions and reject oversized inputs. That changes the amount of memory the application asks to own. Only after those boundaries are explicit does collector tuning become an understandable adjustment rather than an attempt to hide an unbounded workload.

sections.title: Build an experiment with a narrow claim
sections.body:
The downloadable lab holds one twelve-MiB byte buffer alive and repeatedly allocates 512 blocks of 512 KiB: 256 MiB of allocation traffic. A completed collection establishes the starting point before the allocation loop. The program records collection counts and the heap goal at the end of that loop, then collects again before measuring retained memory.

Each setting runs in a fresh process three times. The runtime version, architecture, GOMAXPROCS, environment settings and raw JSON are recorded. The large buffers contain bytes rather than pointers to other heap objects. That matters: this experiment is intentionally not a model of a pointer-rich object cache, a concurrent web service, or a memory-intensive native library.

```sh
go build -o memlab ./cmd/memlab
GOGC=50 ./memlab -mode gc
GOGC=100 ./memlab -mode gc
GOGC=200 ./memlab -mode gc
GOGC=200 GOMEMLIMIT=32MiB ./memlab -mode gc
```

Before comparing runs, clear an inherited GOMEMLIMIT when testing the cases without a limit. The lab runner does this explicitly. An unnoticed environment setting can otherwise make two apparently different GOGC runs obey the same effective constraint. The goal is to understand what changed, not merely collect a row of numbers that looks scientific.

sections.title: What this local experiment actually showed
sections.body:
The following table uses medians across three fresh processes. The heap-goal column is the observed target at the end of the allocation loop, not peak memory use or a guaranteed cap. Approximate MiB values are conversions of recorded byte counts.

| GOGC | GOMEMLIMIT | Collections during allocation loop | End-of-loop heap goal |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 50 | not set | 39 | 19.90 MiB |
| 100 | not set | 19 | 26.60 MiB |
| 200 | not set | 8 | 55.00 MiB |
| 200 | 32 MiB | 21 | 25.88 MiB |

The collector ran less frequently when more headroom was allowed in this workload. Adding a soft limit constrained that relationship. After an explicit final collection, every case still retained roughly the same twelve-MiB application buffer. No setting made that reachable buffer disappear.

The loop's measured durations were only a few milliseconds. That is too short and narrow a test to establish a production performance ranking. We deliberately do not turn them into a claim that one setting makes a service faster. Background activity, allocator behavior and the synthetic workload matter. Likewise, the observed targets do not need to equal a formula evaluated from the final heap: the pacer uses collection history and the runtime is operating concurrently.

The useful result is the relationship between headroom, collection frequency and unchanged live ownership. For production, repeat the experiment with representative object lifetimes, concurrency and latency measurements before selecting a setting.

sections.title: Distinguish collector work from application allocation work
sections.body:
A CPU increase can involve allocating and initializing objects, tracing reachable objects, reclaiming memory, synchronization, or unrelated application work. A single GC-cycle count cannot identify which part dominates. A lower number of collections is not automatically a lower end-to-end cost, just as fewer database queries do not automatically mean a faster endpoint.

Use CPU profiles and runtime observations together. The [diagnostics guide](https://go.dev/doc/diagnostics) describes the available profiling tools. A useful investigation follows the allocation site back to the operation that creates demand: a temporary conversion, a per-item map, a repeated string representation or an unnecessarily retained response buffer.

For the document API, compare equivalent outputs. Removing an allocation by dropping a validation step is not an optimization of the same behavior. Reusing a mutable buffer without giving callers independent ownership can improve a microbenchmark while corrupting concurrent responses. A performance change needs a correctness test as well as a resource measurement.

Our [allocation-profiling lab](/news/go-allocation-profiling-pprof-escape-benchmarks) includes a revealing counterexample: a faster formatting implementation that still performs the same number of result allocations. That is a useful improvement in one dimension, but it is not evidence that GC traffic disappeared. Separate the claim you measured from the claim you hoped to prove.

sections.title: Measure roots and scannable data deliberately
sections.body:
A large byte buffer and a collection of small pointer-rich nodes can occupy similar numbers of bytes while presenting different tracing work. Roots also matter: stacks and globals can keep object graphs reachable. Increasing the number of concurrent operations can therefore change both retained state and the set of roots the runtime must consider.

The [runtime/metrics catalog](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/metrics) exposes measurements for scannable heap space, stack scanning and globals. Those measurements have different definitions and should not all be interpreted as the number of bytes actually visited during an arbitrary request. Preserve the metric names and read the matching toolchain's descriptions before constructing a ratio.

For example, /gc/scan/heap:bytes describes scannable heap space. It is not a direct count of pointer edges, a heap-depth limit or a duration. A large pointer-free payload can contribute heavily to live bytes without contributing the same amount of pointer-bearing content. That does not make it free: it still occupies memory and participates in allocation and object bookkeeping.

A practical cache review should therefore ask what each entry retains, how entries reference each other, and how the cache is bounded. The [reachability lesson](/learn/runtime.gc-reachability) is a better starting point for that review than searching for a collector flag that promises to ignore application-owned objects.

sections.title: Avoid making manual collection part of every request
sections.body:
The lab calls runtime.GC to establish observation boundaries. That is an experimental control, not a recommendation to force collection after each API request. A manually imposed collection can add work and change the behavior you are trying to observe. It can also distract from the actual problem: the application still retaining the wrong objects or producing avoidable allocation traffic.

Similarly, a single low heap measurement immediately after a forced collection does not describe a workload's peak usage. A service may grow again during the next burst, and the operating system may account for released and reserved memory differently from the heap statistic you sampled. Collect a time series around meaningful workload transitions.

For a batch processor, compare memory before work, during a bounded peak, after completion and after a quiet period. State whether a collection was explicitly requested at each boundary. For a long-running service, prefer a representative observation window and correlate memory with admitted work, completed work and cache size.

If forced collection is part of a justified operational procedure, document why, how frequently it runs and what outcome it is expected to change. Treat it as a measured intervention with costs, not a universal cleanup button whose successful return proves that the process is now small.

sections.title: Turn tuning into a controlled rollout
sections.body:
Change one variable at a time. First establish the workload envelope and correctness tests, then capture a baseline. Apply a collector setting to a limited deployment slice and compare useful completions, latency, runtime memory and collection pressure under equivalent demand. Keep a rollback value and a stopping condition.

Do not compare a quiet weekday baseline with a busy release window and attribute the whole difference to GOGC. Note payload distribution, cache warmup, replica count and background jobs. A change that works with a cold cache may behave differently after the live object graph has grown. A setting that looks good on a native desktop may be inappropriate in a constrained container or an app sandbox.

Use the service's own availability objective. If a lower memory allowance creates sustained collection pressure and harms request completion, that is not a successful memory optimization merely because a graph has a lower ceiling. Conversely, accepting more memory to reduce CPU may be reasonable only if the deployment actually has that headroom across all replicas.

The lesson from [bounded work](/learn/concurrency.bounded-work) applies directly: capacity decisions belong to the application and deployment, not only to the collector. A collector policy should support those boundaries, and the rollout should verify that the intended business work still completes.

sections.title: Keep a reproducible memory budget beside the service
sections.body:
A useful handoff includes the selected toolchain, workload shape, live-data expectations, input and concurrency limits, collector settings, raw measurements and a repeatable command. It also explains what was not measured. Our experiment records Go-managed memory and collection behavior; it does not measure production RSS, tail latency, native-library memory or every allocation pattern a real application may produce.

[Download the original memory lab, tests and measurement data](/downloads/go-memory-lab-20261029.zip). The archive includes the GC workload, graph-shape and retention modes, formatting benchmarks and a README. The measurements are small local observations with their methodology attached, not a benchmark leaderboard.

Continue with [GC interview preparation](/interview/runtime.gc), [stack and heap ownership](/learn/runtime.stack-and-heap), and the companion [heap-graph investigation](/news/go-heap-graphs-reachability-retained-memory). When memory behavior becomes confusing, return to the same sequence: identify the owner, bound the work, measure the relevant quantity, change one decision, and verify the outcome. That sequence remains useful even when a future Go release changes the collector's implementation details.

title: Go heap graphs: depth, reachability and retained memory
description: Explore Go heap depth with equal-node chain and tree experiments. Trace roots, compare scannable memory, and fix a tiny slice retaining a 16 MiB backing array.

sections.title: Heap size is not the same question as heap depth
sections.body:
When someone asks how deep a Go heap can become, several different questions may be hiding inside the phrase. They might mean the depth of a linked object graph, the amount of retained memory, the depth of a recursive call stack, or the amount of pointer-bearing data the collector must inspect. Those quantities are related in an application, but they are not interchangeable runtime settings.

Consider a service that stores a hierarchy of documents. One representation is a long chain of nodes; another is a balanced tree. A separate bug keeps a tiny slice of a large input buffer in every cached result. The hierarchy may have a dramatically different logical depth in the two representations while the slice bug, which has almost no visible graph depth, dominates retained bytes. Optimizing the wrong quantity produces an elegant data structure without fixing the memory incident.

This guide investigates those distinctions with two original experiments: equal-sized node graphs and a small view retaining a large backing array. The lab ran with native Go 1.27.3 on darwin/arm64, Apple M4, GOMAXPROCS two. Each case used a fresh process. The data and complete sources are downloadable; the results are observations about those controlled programs, not a universal ranking of linked lists and trees.

sections.title: Trace ownership from a root to an object
sections.body:
An object remains live when the running program can still reach it through the relevant roots and references. A reference can be indirect: a global cache points to an entry, the entry points to a closure, and the closure keeps a large buffer reachable. Removing one local variable does not break that entire ownership path if another path still exists.

The official [GC guide](https://go.dev/doc/gc-guide) introduces reachability and roots. Use that model to ask a concrete question during an incident: which owner still has a reason to access this object? An object can be reachable even when the application will never use it again. The collector preserves the program's reachable state; it does not infer the business meaning of an expired cache entry.

Unreachable cycles are not automatically permanent leaks. A cycle with no remaining root path is different from a cycle held in a global registry. In the first case, circular references alone do not create an application owner. In the second, the registry does. Drawing the incoming root edge often explains the incident more clearly than drawing every link inside the cycle.

Start with the [reachability lesson](/learn/runtime.gc-reachability), then annotate a real ownership path: who adds an entry, who removes it, and what event establishes that removal is safe. Those answers connect lifetime semantics to code that a reviewer can inspect.

sections.title: Separate call-stack depth from object-graph depth
sections.body:
A deeply recursive function can create a deep call stack. A deeply linked heap structure can exist even when the program traverses it iteratively. The stack-depth problem belongs to the traversal algorithm and its execution; the graph-depth problem belongs to the stored relationships. A change from recursion to iteration does not automatically change which heap objects remain reachable.

Our graph validator uses an explicit work list rather than recursively visiting a hundred thousand nodes. That makes the validation independent of a recursive call chain of the same depth. The helper is deliberately limited to the acyclic chain and tree produced by the lab; it is not a general-purpose graph walker that detects arbitrary cycles.

The [stack-and-heap lesson](/learn/runtime.stack-and-heap) explains the ownership distinction. Avoid simplistic rules such as all local variables live on the stack or returning a pointer always establishes one fixed allocation cost. Compiler decisions, object size, inlining and how a value is used affect the actual program. For allocation placement, inspect the selected compiler and measure the built workload.

Most importantly, do not look for one heap-depth switch that solves all three problems: recursive stack growth, retained data and collector work. A robust investigation names the quantity it is measuring before choosing the tool or changing the representation.

sections.title: Compare equal node types before comparing shapes
sections.body:
The graph experiment allocates one hundred thousand objects of exactly the same Node type in each case. Every node has two pointer fields and a fixed payload. Both graphs have one root and exactly one fewer non-nil edges than nodes. The chain uses one child link per node; the balanced tree distributes those same edges across two child fields.

```go
type Node struct {
    Left, Right *Node
    Payload [48]byte
}
```

Construction temporarily uses an index slice so that the requested topology can be built easily. The lab does not return that slice. It performs a collection after construction and validation before taking the graph measurements. Otherwise the index would keep every node directly reachable and add a different ownership structure to the experiment.
