This control matters more than the choice of an impressive-looking graph size. A comparison that changes the node type, object count, payload size and root count simultaneously cannot isolate the meaning of depth. Even our controlled comparison changes edge placement and locality together with logical depth, so it cannot establish that depth alone caused a timing difference.

```sh
go build -o memlab ./cmd/memlab
GOGC=100 ./memlab -mode chain
GOGC=100 ./memlab -mode tree
```

The program prints node count and logical depth alongside memory observations. That lets a reader verify what was constructed before interpreting what the runtime measured.

sections.title: What the graph experiment showed
sections.body:
The table reports medians from three fresh processes for each shape. Byte deltas are measured after collection relative to a pre-construction baseline. The scannable-heap value comes from the runtime metric with that definition; it is not a stopwatch measurement or an exact count of live pointer edges.

| Shape | Nodes | Logical depth | Retained heap delta | Scannable heap delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Chain | 100,000 | 100,000 | 6,409,896 bytes | 1,600,328 bytes |
| Balanced tree | 100,000 | 17 | 6,409,992 bytes | 1,600,416 bytes |

The logical depths were very different while these two memory quantities were almost identical in this experiment. That is the useful structural result. It does not prove identical collection latency. The lab also timed seven complete forced collections per process: the median of those process medians was about 1.501 milliseconds for the chain and 0.624 milliseconds for the tree in this run.

Those timings include more than pure pointer scanning. The experiment is small, sequential and not a randomized production benchmark; locality, work distribution and system activity can influence it. We preserve the raw rounds instead of promoting the ratio into a general rule that trees make Go GC a particular amount faster. Equal bytes do not imply identical runtime behavior, and different depths do not by themselves explain every observed difference.

sections.title: Bytes and pointer-bearing content describe different costs
sections.body:
A payload consisting of bytes does not contain the same reference structure as a collection of pointer-rich objects. Both occupy memory, but they do not present identical tracing work. Conversely, a compact object can retain a large amount of other data through its references. The size of the owner is not the size of everything it keeps alive.

The [runtime/metrics reference](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/metrics) defines /gc/scan/heap:bytes as scannable heap space. Keep that definition separate from live heap bytes, object count and collection duration. A metric that sounds like scanning is not automatically a measurement of work performed during the request you are investigating.

For a cache design, inspect representation as well as capacity. Can an entry store a compact identifier rather than a reference to a large request object? Does a shared index keep an entire graph alive after individual entries expire? Is a byte blob large but pointer-free, or does an object contain many relationships that must remain traversable?

These questions do not imply that pointers are bad or that every structure should be flattened. Pointer-based structures can make mutation and ownership clearer. The right comparison includes access patterns, correctness, allocation behavior and measured collector effects. Our [GC tuning guide](/news/go-garbage-collector-gogc-gomemlimit-lab) explains why changing a collector percentage cannot replace those design decisions.

sections.title: A thirty-two-byte view can retain sixteen MiB
sections.body:
The second experiment allocates a sixteen-MiB backing array and returns only its first thirty-two bytes. One mode keeps the ordinary view. Another uses a full-slice expression to restrict capacity to thirty-two. The third copies the prefix into independent storage. All three modes return the same visible byte contents.

The [slice specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types) explains the relationship between a slice and its underlying array. Restricting capacity changes what later reslicing and appending can do through that slice; it does not create an independent backing allocation. The [slices.Clip contract](https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Clip) is useful when reviewing that distinction.

| Result mode | Visible length | Visible capacity | Post-GC heap delta, median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| View | 32 | 16,777,216 | 16,786,976 bytes |
| Capacity clipped | 32 | 32 | 16,786,960 bytes |
| Independent copy | 32 | 32 | 9,776 bytes |

These deltas include small runtime and experiment overheads; the last row does not mean a thirty-two-byte result intrinsically needs 9,776 bytes. The large difference is the retained backing array. The example gives a concrete reason to ask which storage a small result owns, rather than assuming its length describes its retained footprint.

sections.title: Copy at a lifetime boundary, not automatically everywhere
Look for hidden owners in closures, queues and registries
sections.body:
A retention investigation should follow more than obvious struct fields. A closure can capture a large input. A buffered channel can retain queued messages. A blocked goroutine can keep values needed by its suspended work. A registry can preserve an object after the feature that created it has already finished.

For example, a callback that returns a small prefix may still capture the original buffer. Moving the callback into a cache extends that buffer's lifetime even if the caller drops every direct slice reference. The fix may be to capture an independent result, bound the cache or remove the callback at the correct lifecycle event. Which change is correct depends on the feature's contract.

Separate useful retained work from abandoned work. A queue containing ten deliberately admitted jobs is different from an unbounded queue accepting requests faster than workers can finish. A goroutine intentionally waiting for its owner is different from a goroutine whose owner has disappeared. Collector tuning does not provide the missing admission limit or cancellation path.

Use [goroutine ownership and leak investigation](/news/go-1-27-goroutine-leak-profiles) and [bounded work](/learn/concurrency.bounded-work) together with heap profiles. The allocation site tells you where an object came from; the application ownership path explains why it is still there. Both are needed before removing or changing the object safely.

sections.title: Pools and weak references do not remove lifetime design
sections.body:
A sync.Pool is a reuse mechanism with a specific contract, not a durable cache with an application-defined byte ceiling. The [sync.Pool documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#Pool) allows stored items to be removed. Code must remain correct if a requested reusable item is unavailable. Conversely, retaining very large buffers for possible reuse can keep capacity associated with a workload after the useful request has ended.

Choose a reuse policy with an explicit size boundary when the workload needs one. Rejecting oversized buffers from a reuse path may be more understandable than treating every previously allocated capacity as valuable. Test correctness without relying on a particular object being returned by the pool.

Weak references can support specialized cache designs, but they change what the cache promises. The [weak package](https://pkg.go.dev/weak) is not a substitute for deterministic resource release, and a weakly held value may be unavailable when requested. The Go team's [cleanup and weak-reference article](https://go.dev/blog/cleanups-and-weak) discusses these lower-level tools and their constraints.

For files, transactions, sockets and other externally limited resources, keep explicit ownership and cleanup. A garbage collector decides memory reachability, not the business deadline for releasing a connection or closing a descriptor. Do not make an operational resource budget depend on when an unreachable object happens to be collected.

sections.title: Validate reachability experiments without measuring compiler accidents
sections.body:
The lab keeps the result alive through the measurement boundary with runtime.KeepAlive. This is important because a value can stop being needed by the program before the end of a source-level scope. The [runtime contract](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime#KeepAlive) explains the purpose of the call. In this experiment it helps ensure that the object whose retention we want to measure remains relevant until the observation is complete.

KeepAlive is not a mutex, a general lifetime extension for unrelated objects or a way to repair unsafe concurrent access. It simply belongs to the experiment's ownership boundary. Likewise, forcing GC establishes a controlled observation point here; it does not represent normal request-level service behavior.

Use fresh processes to reduce contamination from previous experiment modes. Validate the graph and result contents before interpreting the memory numbers. Record the runtime, architecture and environment, and preserve raw measurements rather than just a rounded chart. If a result changes after a toolchain update, begin by reproducing the same program and checking which assumption changed.

The test suite checks the graph construction and copy semantics separately from the memory observations. That separation makes a failure easier to interpret: an incorrect graph is not evidence about GC, and a noisy timing is not evidence that the graph's ownership contract is wrong.

sections.title: Turn heap evidence into an ownership change
sections.body:
An actionable memory investigation ends with a specific lifetime decision. Perhaps a cache stores an independent identifier instead of a complete request, a result copies a small prefix before crossing a long-lived boundary, or a queue stops admitting work beyond a documented budget. Verify that the change preserves the feature and reduces the quantity that was actually causing trouble.

[Download the memory lab, raw observations and tests](/downloads/go-memory-lab-20261029.zip). The archive includes equal-node graph construction, iterative validation, retention modes and their methodology. The published timings are local exploratory observations, not a universal collector benchmark or an in-app sandbox certification.

Continue with [heap-retention interview preparation](/interview/runtime.retention), [GC reachability](/learn/runtime.gc-reachability), and [allocation profiles and escape analysis](/news/go-allocation-profiling-pprof-escape-benchmarks). A useful answer to how deep is the heap starts by naming the graph, the roots and the measurement. From there, the practical question is not merely how many links an object has. It is which owner still needs those links and what event allows the retained state to end.

title: Go allocation profiling: pprof, escape analysis and benchmarks
description: Investigate Go allocations with alloc_space and inuse_space profiles, compiler escape analysis and equivalent formatter benchmarks. Includes tested downloadable code.

sections.title: Start with a question that a profile can answer
sections.body:
A Go endpoint becomes expensive after a product change. Its latency increases, allocation charts rise, and somebody proposes replacing every fmt call with a hand-written encoder. That might improve the endpoint, but it might also consume a week while the actual problem remains an unbounded result cache. Before changing code, decide whether the incident concerns allocation traffic, retained memory, CPU time, latency, or a combination of them.

These are different optimization targets. Allocating less over an interval can reduce pressure on the runtime without reducing the long-lived cache. Removing retained objects can reduce the live heap while leaving request-level allocation traffic unchanged. Faster formatting can save CPU even when every returned string still needs an allocation. A useful investigation keeps those claims separate and tests the behavior that users actually receive.

This guide walks through an original memory-profile experiment and a pair of equivalent formatting benchmarks. The lab uses native Go 1.27.3 on darwin/arm64, Apple M4, with GOMAXPROCS two. It includes source, tests, raw observations and commands. These local observations are a reproducible learning exercise, not a claim about every service or the execution characteristics of GopherForge's app sandbox.

sections.title: Understand allocation traffic and retained memory separately
sections.body:
Imagine a worker that creates two thousand temporary blocks while keeping a small sample of them in a result. Almost all of its allocation traffic can disappear from the live heap after collection. A different worker might allocate very little during the same observation window while retaining a large cache created earlier. Looking only at one memory chart cannot distinguish those programs.

The [runtime/pprof documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/pprof) describes the heap profile and its relationship to completed garbage collection. The profile includes sample types that let tools examine allocation history and retained allocations. Use alloc_space to investigate sampled allocated bytes and inuse_space to investigate sampled bytes still in use at the profile's collection boundary. Neither view is a complete ownership graph.

The allocation stack answers where storage was created. It does not necessarily identify the field, queue, closure or registry that currently owns it. A parser can appear prominently in a retained-memory profile because another component stores its results indefinitely. Deleting the parser's allocation would change the feature; changing the retention policy may solve the actual incident.

Read the companion [heap-graph investigation](/news/go-heap-graphs-reachability-retained-memory) when an apparently small result holds a large backing allocation. Read the [GC controls lab](/news/go-garbage-collector-gogc-gomemlimit-lab) when collection pressure is being confused with application ownership.

sections.title: Construct a profile whose expected outcome is known
sections.body:
Our profile mode allocates 2,048 blocks of 64 KiB, for 128 MiB of application payload allocation. It keeps every 128th block, so sixteen blocks remain reachable: exactly one MiB of retained payload. Separate helper functions name the retained and temporary paths. The experiment clears its temporary reference and requests completed collections before writing the profile.

That design gives the profile an independently checkable expectation. Allocation traffic should be dominated by the temporary path, while retained application payload should be associated with the retained path. The program also uses runtime.KeepAlive after the observation boundary so that its retained result remains relevant throughout the measurement.

```sh
go build -o memlab ./cmd/memlab
./memlab -mode profile -out heap.pprof
go tool pprof -top -sample_index=alloc_space ./memlab heap.pprof
go tool pprof -top -sample_index=inuse_space ./memlab heap.pprof
```

The experiment sets the memory-profile sampling rate to 64 KiB before creating its workload. This improves the detail available for a small demonstration, but it changes profiling overhead and does not turn a sampled profile into an exact allocation ledger. Keep the chosen rate beside the results. Do not copy the setting into a production process without considering the observation cost.

sections.title: Read the two profile views without inventing precision
sections.body:
In the recorded run, pprof's alloc_space report printed about 127.91 MB total. The temporary churn helper accounted for 126.85 MB and the retained helper for 0.99 MB. The inuse_space report printed about 1,077.47 kB total, with 1,012.46 kB attributed to the retained helper. These are the units and sampled estimates printed by pprof, rather than exact byte counts reconstructed from the source.

| Question | Profile view | Main application allocation site in this run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where did allocation traffic originate? | alloc_space | churnBlock: 126.85 MB |
| Which allocated payload remains represented? | inuse_space | retainedBlock: 1,012.46 kB |
| How much payload did the program intentionally retain? | Source-level invariant | 16 × 64 KiB = 1 MiB |

The [Go performance guidance](https://go.dev/wiki/Performance) explains the sampling nature of memory profiles. Small runtime allocations and statistical estimation help explain why the printed profile is not identical to the source-level invariant. The reliable conclusion is the separation of temporary traffic from retained payload, not a promise that every run prints those same decimals.

An important negative conclusion follows: a quiet temporary allocation site in inuse_space does not prove that site is cheap. It may still create substantial allocation traffic and CPU work. Likewise, a prominent retained site does not prove a leak. Retention may be intentional and correctly bounded. Follow the profile with an ownership and workload review.

sections.title: Capture profiles at comparable lifecycle boundaries
sections.body:
An incident investigation needs to state when the profile was captured. Was the cache cold or warm? Had requests finished? Was a collection explicitly requested? Was the process still admitting work? A profile taken during startup cannot be compared casually with one taken after several hours of accumulated application state.

For a batch service, choose boundaries such as before the batch, after a representative batch, and after results have been released. For a long-running endpoint, record request volume, payload sizes, active operations and cache entries around the observation window. If the workload changes, a larger allocation total may reflect more completed useful work rather than a regression.

The [Go diagnostics guide](https://go.dev/doc/diagnostics) provides a broader map of profiling tools. Use CPU profiles for CPU attribution and memory profiles for their defined allocation views. A heap profile cannot establish tail latency, and an allocation benchmark cannot establish how an entire service behaves under concurrent load.

If you expose the [net/http/pprof handlers](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/pprof), keep diagnostics on an appropriately restricted management surface. Profiles can contain implementation details and observations about a running service. The downloadable lab writes a local profile file instead, making the learning exercise independent of network configuration or a public diagnostics endpoint.

sections.title: Compare implementations that return the same result
Use a benchmark harness that preserves useful work
sections.body:
The benchmark fixture uses the identifier 123456789 and the value true. It assigns the returned string to a package-level sink and reports allocations. Both implementations use the same fixture, result destination and loop structure. Setup stays outside the timed loop.

```go
var result string

func BenchmarkAppend(b *testing.B) {
    b.ReportAllocs()
    for b.Loop() {
        result = AppendEvent(123456789, true)
    }
}
```

The [testing.B.Loop documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/testing#B.Loop) describes its timing and compiler-preservation behavior. Use its supported loop form rather than assuming any hand-written wrapper has equivalent properties. The global sink also makes the intended observable result explicit in this example.

```sh
GOMAXPROCS=2 go test -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(Format|Append)$' \
  -benchmem -benchtime=150ms -count=5
```

Record the toolchain and machine with the output. The [Go testing flags](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Testing_flags) define the benchmark controls. Repeated runs help reveal variation, but five short repetitions on one machine do not establish a production performance distribution. Change the fixture deliberately when evaluating different identifier sizes, output lengths or workload mixes.

sections.title: A faster formatter can have the same allocation count
sections.body:
The five recorded baseline timings were 51.91, 46.51, 47.36, 45.76 and 45.97 ns/op. The append version produced 12.50, 12.36, 12.19, 12.09 and 12.12 ns/op. Their medians were 46.51 and 12.19 ns/op respectively. Every recorded run reported 24 B/op and one allocation per operation for both implementations.

| Implementation | Median of five runs | Reported bytes per operation | Reported allocations per operation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fmt.Sprintf | 46.51 ns/op | 24 | 1 |
| strconv append operations | 12.19 ns/op | 24 | 1 |

This is useful evidence for a specific CPU-oriented improvement in a specific fixture. It is not evidence that the alternative removed the returned string's allocation. The benchmark records both dimensions precisely because the attractive headline, faster formatting, could otherwise be mistaken for a different claim, less allocation traffic.

Do not generalize the observed timing ratio to whole requests. If formatting accounts for a small fraction of endpoint CPU, even a substantial improvement there may barely affect end-to-end latency. A service waiting on its database will not become several times faster merely because this isolated formatter does. Use a representative CPU profile to estimate whether the local improvement addresses a meaningful cost.

sections.title: Use escape analysis to explain, not replace, measurements
sections.body:
Build the package with compiler diagnostics and inspect the messages for the actual source version. The [compiler documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/compile) describes the diagnostic flag. Decisions can change with inlining, surrounding code, compiler updates and how the result is used.

```sh
go build -gcflags=-m=2 .
```

For the recorded Go 1.27.3 build, the compiler reported that make([]byte, 0, 48) in AppendEvent did not escape and that string(buf) escaped to the heap. Those diagnostics are consistent with the benchmark's single result allocation. The complete diagnostic output is included with the experiment, so the explanation can be checked against the selected compiler rather than remembered as a permanent language rule.

Do not count every line containing escapes as one executed allocation. A diagnostic describes an analysis decision at a source location, not a runtime event counter. A path may execute conditionally, a call may be inlined differently, and surrounding optimization can change the final behavior. Use benchmark allocation counts and profiles to measure the built workload.

The [stack-and-heap lesson](/learn/runtime.stack-and-heap) and [escape-analysis interview guide](/interview/runtime.escape) cover the broader reasoning. The practical habit is simple: form a hypothesis with diagnostics, then verify its effect with equivalent behavior and actual measurements.

sections.title: Avoid changing ownership to win a benchmark
sections.body:
A tempting next step is to return a view into a reusable buffer. That can reduce a local allocation count while allowing a later call to overwrite an earlier result. The benchmark may improve precisely because the implementation stopped providing independent ownership. Such a change needs a different API contract, not a celebratory allocation chart.

If callers can consume bytes synchronously before the next mutation, an append-to-caller-buffer API can be appropriate. If callers store the returned value, independent storage may be necessary. A zero-copy technique is valuable only when its lifetime and mutation restrictions fit the application. Make those restrictions visible in names, documentation and tests.

The [buffer and pool ownership guide](/news/go-bytes-buffer-sync-pool-ownership) explains why reuse requires a clear handoff. Pooling also has its own memory and concurrency tradeoffs. Reusing an oversized buffer can preserve capacity long after a small request ends, while incorrect reuse can corrupt output across operations.

Treat a changed ownership contract as an architectural decision. Test that a previous result remains valid after a subsequent call, and test concurrent usage if the API promises it. Allocation reduction is not a sufficient acceptance criterion when the feature depends on stable independently owned results.

sections.title: Check the workload level before rolling out a local win
sections.body:
A benchmark operation and a user request are not necessarily the same unit of work. An endpoint might format one event, a thousand events, or no events on its common path. Record that relationship before translating nanoseconds per operation into a capacity estimate. Also ask whether the formatter is on the critical path or runs after the response has already completed.

Consider an illustrative calculation, not another measurement from this lab. If formatting consumes five percent of request CPU and a replacement makes that component four times faster, the total CPU reduction is only 3.75 percent under otherwise identical conditions. The remaining ninety-five percent has not changed. Waiting time, contention and request concurrency introduce additional effects that this arithmetic does not model. This helps explain why a clear microbenchmark improvement can produce a modest service-level result.

Build a small fixture matrix before rollout: short and maximum-width identifiers, both boolean values, ordinary and unusually large batches, and the actual destination used by the caller. Keep the correctness suite independent from the timing suite. A rare input can be essential to correctness even when it should not dominate a representative timing fixture.

Finally, compare useful completed operations under equivalent demand. A deployment that reports fewer allocated bytes because it rejected more requests has changed throughput as well as memory use. Preserve acceptance rates, error rates, payload distribution and latency beside resource measurements. Those observations let the team decide whether the local optimization improved the feature that motivated the investigation.

sections.title: Build a repeatable optimization decision
sections.body:
An actionable performance change includes the original symptom, a representative fixture, an explicit result contract, a baseline, the modified implementation and a recheck of correctness and resources. Preserve raw outputs. Explain which dimension improved and which dimensions were unchanged or not measured. Include a rollback path if the change affects a production service.

The lab tests also support deliberately broken variants as negative controls. Returning an aliased prefix must fail the independence test. Removing a separator must fail the formatting equivalence test. Disconnecting a graph node must fail structural validation. These checks make sure the test suite can reject meaningful defects rather than merely run successfully against its own implementation.

[Download the original memory lab, tests and raw observations](/downloads/go-memory-lab-20261029.zip). Start with the profile modes, reproduce the formatting comparison, then change one fixture at a time. Keep native desktop measurements separate from app-sandbox behavior and from production service limits.

Continue with [profiles and leak investigation](/learn/runtime.profiles-and-leaks), [GC budgets](/learn/runtime.gc-budget), and the companion [heap ownership article](/news/go-heap-graphs-reachability-retained-memory). A strong optimization report does not promise that allocations are universally bad. It shows which cost mattered, why the change preserves behavior, and what the measured evidence actually supports.

title: Go streaming I/O: EOF, byte limits and JSON boundaries
description: Handle final bytes with EOF, reject oversized input, validate one JSON document and configure Scanner. Tested Go examples with a hands-on Playground exercise.

sections.title: A stream is not a complete application message
sections.body:
A CSV importer works in a small test and silently drops the final record in production. An HTTP endpoint accepts the first JSON object in a request and ignores a second object after it. A log processor reports success after a long line stops its scanner. These failures look unrelated, but each confuses one boundary with another: a read call, an input budget, a token, a document, or a completed business operation.

This guide builds a practical model for those boundaries. The objective is not to replace every standard helper with a custom loop. It is to understand what the helper promises and what the application must still decide. Reading bytes successfully does not establish that the message was complete, valid, small enough, or safe to commit to a database.

The downloadable lab contains original standard-library examples and tests. We checked it with native Go 1.27.3 and also built its demonstration programs for wasip1/wasm. Cross-compilation checks the target build; it does not establish production throughput or certify execution in every app sandbox. The examples use in-memory input, so their behavior is reproducible without a remote server or an account.

sections.title: Preserve the bytes that arrive with the final error
Distinguish truncating a stream from rejecting oversized input
Make the boundary test matrix explicit
sections.body:
A useful size test covers an empty payload, a zero-byte allowance, one byte below the limit, exactly the limit, and one byte above it. It also covers an underlying reader failure. Our helper returns no accepted payload when the transport fails or the size exceeds the budget. A different application may deliberately expose partial data, but it must label that result as partial rather than silently accept it as complete.

| Input | Limit | Expected result |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Empty | 0 | Accepted empty payload |
| One byte | 0 | Oversized input |
| Three bytes | 4 | Complete payload |
| Four bytes | 4 | Complete payload |
| Five bytes | 4 | Oversized input |

The off-by-one case matters because a superficially safe implementation can simply truncate five bytes to four and return success. The lab includes a negative control that changes max plus one to max; the boundary test must then fail. That proves the test can distinguish rejection from truncation.

For an importer, add a business-level assertion: no record is committed after an incomplete document is rejected. A function can return the right error while another component has already persisted half the input. Unit tests for byte handling and integration tests for effects answer different questions, and both boundaries should remain visible in the design.

sections.title: Require exactly the document your endpoint promises
Separate structural decoding from business validation
sections.body:
Our Event has a required, nonempty identifier. Successfully decoding null or an empty object does not satisfy that requirement. The helper validates the resulting identifier before returning an accepted event. The tests include null, an empty object, an unknown field, malformed input, trailing text and a second complete value.

DisallowUnknownFields is useful for this specific schema policy, but it is not a general strictness certificate. The lab deliberately shows a duplicate identifier field being accepted with the later string value. That example prevents readers from assuming that one decoder option rejects every kind of ambiguity. If duplicate-key rejection is part of the protocol, implement and test that separate policy with an appropriate parser or token-level validation.

The business decision should also consider clients. Rejecting newly introduced fields may be desirable for a small internal command, but it can impede a deliberately forward-compatible event format. A required field may need a separate presence representation when an empty value is meaningful. Those choices belong in an API contract and its compatibility tests.

Keep validation before irreversible effects whenever the operation requires atomic acceptance. If a large import intentionally commits incrementally, give records explicit identifiers, document partial completion, and define retry behavior. A parser cannot retroactively make an already committed batch atomic simply by returning an error at the end.

sections.title: Understand token limits before choosing Scanner
Buffered output has its own completion boundary
sections.body:
Successful input parsing does not establish that output reached its destination. A report generator may write several small rows into a buffered writer and receive no immediate error because the bytes are still held locally. The later flush can fail. The [bufio writer reference](https://pkg.go.dev/bufio#Writer) describes the buffering and flush operations; the feature must decide when it is allowed to report completion.

The lab tests that distinction with an in-memory destination. Before Flush, the destination has no bytes; afterward it contains the expected payload. A separate destination returns an error, and the test requires that Flush expose the failure. This makes a late output failure reproducible without a network service or a full disk.

Keep the completion claim precise. A successful flush through one layer proves that layer accepted the operation under its contract. It does not automatically prove durable storage, remote processing or a committed business transaction. If those stronger guarantees matter, obtain and test the corresponding acknowledgement at that boundary.

For the importer, this creates a useful pair of questions: did the input form a complete accepted message, and did its intended effect complete successfully? Returning success only after the right acknowledgements prevents a byte-processing helper from accidentally defining the business transaction.

sections.title: Budget transformations as well as incoming bytes
sections.body:
An input may pass through decompression, decoding, normalization and object construction before the application uses it. A small compressed representation does not establish a small decoded representation. The [gzip reader reference](https://pkg.go.dev/compress/gzip#Reader) defines the decompression layer; the service still needs a budget for the data produced by that layer.

For a compressed upload, distinguish wire-byte limits from decoded-byte limits. Place limits where their meanings are clear, preserve the original error, and explain which budget failed. Add a processing deadline and concurrency limit when the endpoint needs them. A byte ceiling alone does not stop a peer from delivering acceptable bytes indefinitely slowly.

The [HTTP MaxBytesReader API](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#MaxBytesReader) provides request-body-specific behavior and a size error. Our native tests exercise it with an in-memory request reader and recorder; they do not start a network listener. A real HTTP endpoint should select a status policy and avoid exposing internal diagnostics as its public response.

These controls complement [backpressure and bounded work](/news/go-backpressure-concurrency-limits-queues-deadlines). A service that admits unlimited concurrent bounded requests can still exceed its overall capacity. Describe per-message limits and system-wide admission separately so that operators know which quantity each setting controls.

sections.title: Keep cancellation and cleanup attached to the owner
sections.body:
Wrapping a generic reader with a context check between reads does not guarantee that an already blocked Read can be interrupted. The transport or underlying implementation needs an actual cancellation mechanism, deadline or owned close operation. The [context package](https://pkg.go.dev/context) supplies cancellation signals; arbitrary I/O implementations do not automatically observe them.

For a request handler, identify who owns the body and any transformation layers. For a background import, identify who closes the source when the job ends and who waits for workers to exit. An abandoned goroutine holding a reader can preserve both memory and an external resource even after its caller has returned an error.

Avoid deferring cleanup only inside an unbounded outer loop when the resource should end after each record or file. Extract a smaller operation with a clear lifetime if that makes ownership explicit. If cleanup can fail, decide whether it changes the operation's outcome or belongs in a separate diagnostic path.

The [cancel-and-join lesson](/learn/concurrency.cancel-and-join) connects the signal to actual completion. The companion [time and deadline guide](/news/go-time-utc-dst-monotonic-deadlines) explains why a finite timeout and a business calendar deadline are different contracts. Neither a cancellation signal nor a byte limit proves the worker has actually finished.

sections.title: Try the failure cases in GopherForge Playground
sections.body:
[Download the complete I/O and time lab](/downloads/go-boundaries-lab-20261029.zip), then open its streamio/main.go. The program is self-contained and uses standard-library packages. In [GopherForge Playground](/playground), download your current source copy before replacing any existing draft, select main.go and paste the demonstration. Keep your own go.mod in the project. Editing the browser draft does not execute Go.

When you want to share an experiment, create a temporary room deliberately. Open that room in a compatible GopherForge app and press the local Run button on the device where execution should happen. Other participants receive device-labelled output for that source revision. Creating a room uploads its source to the relay; simply reading this article does not publish an example or create a room. The [MCP guide](/guide/mcp) explains the capability links and expiry.

Change the payload from four bytes to five while keeping the budget at four. Add a second JSON object, then replace it with whitespace. Increase the scanner's line length past its configured allowance. Before each run, write down the expected accepted value or error. Compare that prediction with the actual output rather than merely checking that the compiler accepted the program.

If Claude or Codex helps, ask it to propose one input mutation and predict the output without running anything. Review its source edit, press Run yourself, and compare the reported revision. This makes the exercise interactive while keeping execution under the local user's control.

sections.title: Test the envelope and the effect independently
sections.body:
Run the full suite with go test rather than inferring correctness from a successful demonstration printout. The native tests exercise small destination buffers, exact limits, oversized data, transport failure, JSON suffixes, required values, duplicate-key behavior and Scanner errors. They also check the HTTP size-error type. The published output is an observation from the included source, not a promise that every library error string remains identical across toolchains.

```sh
go test -race -count=50 ./...
go run ./streamio
```

For a real importer, add controlled destination failures and assertions about committed work. Decide whether a failed operation can be retried, whether its record identifiers are idempotent, and how partial completion is reported. Those are application-level contracts outside the small byte-reading helper.

The [buffer-ownership article](/news/go-bytes-buffer-sync-pool-ownership) covers another boundary: whether a result remains valid after a reusable buffer changes. Together, envelope size, framing, ownership and effects give a reviewer a concrete way to assess an input path. The useful question is not simply whether the program streams. It is which boundaries it enforces, which failures it reports, and which useful work remains committed when the stream ends unexpectedly.

title: Go time: UTC, DST, calendar days and reliable deadlines
description: Model Go instants, durations and calendar schedules. Test DST, timezone data, timestamp round trips, timer ownership and deadlines with a downloadable lab.

sections.title: Start by naming the kind of time your feature uses
sections.body:
A daily report moves an hour after a clock change. A timeout survives a JSON round trip but behaves differently from an in-process measurement. Two timestamps print different local hours while describing the same event. These bugs often begin when an application treats an instant, a duration, a civil date and a recurring local schedule as interchangeable values.

Consider a document service with three requirements. A conversion may run for at most thirty seconds. A daily digest should be sent at the customer's chosen local morning time. A published article belongs to an editorial calendar date. The first is an elapsed-work budget, the second is a schedule tied to location rules, and the third is a date label. One helper that adds a fixed number of nanoseconds cannot express all three contracts correctly.

This guide develops those distinctions with an original, reproducible Go lab. Its examples use fixed inputs around offset transitions, explicit locations, cancellation and tests with virtual time. They are engineering examples rather than a universal scheduler. The implementation decisions that remain, including missing and repeated local times, are called out instead of being hidden behind a convenient function name.

sections.title: Separate an instant from its display representation
sections.body:
An instant answers when an event occurred on a timeline. A representation answers how that instant appears in a particular location or format. Our lab constructs a UTC instant and displays the same value in a fixed two-hour offset. The local clock fields differ, but Time.Equal reports that the two values describe the same instant. The == operator compares more representation details and is unsuitable as a casual replacement for that intent.

```go
a := time.Date(2026, 10, 4, 10, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
b := a.In(time.FixedZone("display", 2*60*60))
fmt.Println(a.Equal(b)) // true
fmt.Println(a == b)     // false for these representations
```

The [time package reference](https://pkg.go.dev/time) defines the comparison and location operations. Use a test that states the intended equivalence. If an API accepts differently offset timestamps for the same event, compare the parsed instants. If the application instead groups reports by the customer's local date, extract that date in the selected location and test that separate grouping rule.

Do not normalize away information that the feature needs. Storing an event instant in UTC is useful, but a future recurring morning appointment may also require its named location and recurrence policy. A stored offset alone cannot explain how a later occurrence should respond when civil-time rules change.

The [Duration lesson](/learn/stdlib.time) provides a shorter introduction before the calendar and deadline experiments below.

sections.title: Use calendar arithmetic for a calendar requirement
sections.body:
The lab's NextDay helper uses AddDate to preserve local calendar intent. It deliberately chooses noon, away from the missing or repeated clock times that require a scheduler policy. In Europe/Zurich, the recorded 2026 spring fixture crosses an offset change: the next calendar noon is twenty-three elapsed hours away. The autumn fixture crosses the reverse transition and takes twenty-five elapsed hours.

```go
func NextDay(t time.Time) time.Time {
    return t.AddDate(0, 0, 1)
}

calendar := NextDay(start)
elapsed := start.Add(24 * time.Hour)
```

| Fixture in Europe/Zurich | Next local calendar noon | Elapsed interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 28 March 2026, noon | 29 March 2026, noon | 23 hours |
| 24 October 2026, noon | 25 October 2026, noon | 25 hours |

Adding twenty-four elapsed hours lands at a different local hour in these fixtures. The tests verify both the preserved noon and the interval, rather than relying on a screenshot of a formatted date. These are observations using the recorded toolchain and its available zone rules; they are not a claim that every day in that location has an unusual length.

The practical decision follows the requirement. A timeout for a conversion uses an elapsed duration. A digest scheduled for tomorrow at a local hour uses calendar and location rules. Choosing the wrong operation can create a perfectly valid Go value that violates the feature's contract.

sections.title: Treat missing and repeated local times as product decisions
sections.body:
A midday demonstration does not solve a recurrence scheduled inside a clock transition. Some local clock readings never occur during a forward change; others occur twice during a backward change. A scheduler needs an explicit policy: skip an occurrence, choose a defined interpretation, move it to a valid time, or ask the user. The right behavior depends on the feature and must be documented.

The [IANA time-zone theory](https://data.iana.org/time-zones/tzdb/theory.html) explains why location identifiers represent histories and rule sets rather than simple permanent offsets. Civil-time rules are data that can change. A product promising a local recurring time should preserve the selected location identity and define how updated rules affect future occurrences.

For the document service, distinguish an already scheduled occurrence from the recurrence template that generated it. The occurrence has a concrete instant and delivery state. The template has a local clock preference, location and policy. Updating the template should not accidentally resend an already delivered digest or erase evidence of the previous schedule.

Test the policy at both transition directions and at an ordinary date. Include a rule-data update in the operational plan when future schedules matter. Our NextDay helper remains intentionally smaller: it demonstrates calendar arithmetic at unambiguous noon and does not claim to implement those missing-time, repeated-time or delivery guarantees.

sections.title: Make zone data part of the deployment evidence
sections.body:
A program that loads named locations needs appropriate zone data in its execution environment. The lab imports time/tzdata so its demonstration can use embedded fallback data when external data is unavailable. The [time/tzdata reference](https://pkg.go.dev/time/tzdata) describes that mechanism. The import is an application packaging decision, not a reason for every reusable library to silently change a consumer's binary.

Record the selected Go toolchain and how the production executable obtains location rules. A desktop environment, a small container and a sandbox may have different available files. A successful test on a developer laptop does not prove that the deployed program has the same environment or future update policy.

The native lab was checked with Go 1.27.3. We also cross-compiled its standalone demonstration for wasip1/wasm. That validates the selected target's build, not every runtime behavior of every host. If a particular host lacks or restricts a capability, the correct result is an explicit unsupported or failed operation rather than a fabricated successful observation.

The [runtime packaging lesson](/learn/operations.docker-build) connects this issue to deployment. Shipping an executable is only one part of shipping its operational assumptions. Zone data, certificates, owned storage and configuration all need an intentional source and a way to verify what actually reached the running environment.

sections.title: Distinguish wall-clock timestamps from elapsed measurements
sections.body:
A service needs wall-clock timestamps to describe events to other systems. Measuring how long a local operation takes is a different task. Go's [1.9 release notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.9#monotonic-time) introduced the monotonic-clock support used in time measurements. The key engineering lesson is to keep an in-process elapsed measurement attached to values obtained for that purpose rather than reconstructing it from formatted clock text.

```go
start := time.Now()
performWork()
elapsed := time.Since(start)
```

Formatting, parsing and serialization do not preserve the private process-local measurement context as a portable distributed clock. A JSON timestamp communicates an instant representation, not a monotonic stopwatch that another process can continue exactly. The lab checks that stripping monotonic metadata with Round(0) preserves instant equality; it does not pretend to simulate an operating-system clock correction.

For the conversion timeout, keep the local start and duration in memory while the operation runs. For an audit record, store a timestamp and an explicitly named duration field if both are needed. Avoid overloading one numeric column with values that sometimes mean an epoch timestamp and sometimes mean an elapsed interval.

Across processes, clocks and delivery delays introduce additional uncertainty. A remote timestamp can help explain event ordering under a defined system model, but it is not proof of a precise one-way network latency. Use instrumentation designed for the question and state the assumptions that connect the measurement to the conclusion.

sections.title: Define units and precision at every serialization boundary
sections.body:
An integer timestamp is incomplete documentation unless its unit and epoch are explicit. Seconds, milliseconds and nanoseconds can all fit into the same language-level integer type for some values while meaning radically different dates. A duration field named timeout is similarly ambiguous when one client sends milliseconds and another assumes seconds.

[RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339) provides a standard timestamp representation with offset information. Our example parses one UTC string and one offset string, then verifies that both identify the same instant. This is a useful contract test because the visible local hours differ while the intended event does not.

```text
2026-10-04T10:00:00Z
2026-10-04T12:00:00+02:00
```

Choose and document precision as well as units. If a database or downstream system rounds values, decide whether equality, deduplication and ordering depend on the discarded fraction. Normalize at an agreed boundary and test the round trip through the actual storage or wire format. Comparing a high-precision in-memory value with a rounded persisted value without that policy can create false differences.

For date-only editorial labels, use a date contract rather than inventing a midnight instant and allowing an arbitrary viewer location to move it to the previous day. GopherForge's article edition date and actual publication date are separate labels for separate purposes. That distinction is a small example of a broader modeling rule: choose a representation that preserves the meaning the feature actually needs.

sections.title: Keep an absolute deadline and an attempt timeout distinct
sections.body:
A workflow can have one overall deadline while each dependency call receives a smaller attempt budget. Replacing the overall deadline with a fresh full timeout at every layer can extend the operation beyond the user's allowance. Conversely, applying an expired deadline to a newly scheduled future task can reject useful work immediately. Name the owner and lifetime of each budget.

The [context documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/context) defines deadline and cancellation propagation. A child operation should respect the remaining parent allowance. Releasing a derived context's resources when its work ends is part of ownership. These controls are local execution contracts; a timestamp printed into a queue message does not automatically cancel a worker that never observes it.

For the document service, record the overall conversion allowance, any per-attempt cap and retry admission policy. A retry must have remaining useful time and an appropriate idempotency contract. Do not restart the entire budget simply because the previous attempt reached its own timeout.

Continue with [backpressure and request budgets](/news/go-backpressure-concurrency-limits-queues-deadlines) and the [context-contract lesson](/learn/clean-production.context-contracts). The article on [I/O boundaries](/news/go-streaming-io-reader-eof-limits-json) covers the corresponding resource issue: checking a context between reads does not necessarily interrupt an already blocked arbitrary reader. A timeout declaration needs a real path to the underlying operation.

sections.title: Give timers one owner and check the selected semantics
sections.body:
A timer signals that its condition has become ready; it does not prove that the application handled the signal at an exact wall-clock instant. Scheduling delays and work already in progress can separate timer readiness from useful completion. A stopped timer is also not a general broadcast mechanism for ending every worker that refers to it.

Go's [timer-channel migration notes](https://go.dev/wiki/Go123Timer) describe the changes introduced for Go 1.23 and the role of the main module's Go version and compatibility settings. Check those facts for the actual executable before copying old stop-and-drain recipes or assuming a historical buffered-channel behavior. The lab uses a Go 1.25 module and a current selected toolchain; its behavior is tested in that configuration.

Our Wait helper creates one timer, owns its cleanup, and selects between the timer and context cancellation. It checks an already cancelled context before admitting the wait. If cancellation and timer readiness race later, it does not claim a universal priority between simultaneously ready select cases. The tests deliberately avoid using that race as a business rule.

A real workflow should state what completion means. If cancellation must prevent a side effect, verify the condition at the boundary that authorizes that effect. A select result elsewhere in the program is not an atomic transaction spanning a later database write. This is why timer ownership, cancellation and durable work need related but separate contracts.

sections.title: Test time with fixed inputs and controlled progress
sections.body:
The calendar tests use fixed dates, a named location and exact expected local fields. They do not wait for a real seasonal transition. The equality tests compare representations of a known instant. These pure tests should be fast and explain their failure directly.

For asynchronous behavior, the lab uses testing/synctest to test a five-second timer and a cancelled hour-long wait without sleeping for those wall-clock durations. The Go team's [testing-time article](https://go.dev/blog/testing-time) explains the motivation for controlled asynchronous tests. The tests check completion and join the worker; merely sending cancellation is insufficient evidence that the goroutine has exited.

```sh
go test -race -count=50 ./...
go run ./gotime
```

The negative control replaces calendar addition with a fixed twenty-four-hour addition. The DST test must fail. Another control removes the cancellation branch from Wait; the cancellation-and-join assertion must reject it. These intentionally broken variants show that the tests enforce a meaningful distinction rather than repeat the implementation in another spelling.

For production, add integration tests for the real queue, database or scheduler boundary. Fake-time unit tests do not establish clock synchronization between machines, operating-system suspend behavior, or delivery guarantees. The [synctest guide](/news/go-concurrency-tests-synctest-without-sleeps) explains how to keep deterministic unit tests and real-boundary tests complementary.

sections.title: Explore the model interactively in Playground
sections.body:
[Download the I/O and time lab](/downloads/go-boundaries-lab-20261029.zip) and inspect gotime/main.go. Before editing an existing [Playground](/playground) draft, download your own source copy. Paste the self-contained program into main.go and keep a compatible go.mod. The demonstration uses standard-library imports, including the zone-data fallback, and has no network calls.

Start by predicting the spring and autumn outputs. Change the location, the starting date or the operation, then run the program on your selected native device. A fixed-offset location will not reproduce the same seasonal rule changes; that is a useful contrast when exploring the distinction between an offset and a named location. If loading a location fails, keep the error visible rather than substituting a different location silently.

The browser editor does not execute Go. If you choose to collaborate, create a temporary room, open it in a compatible GopherForge app and press its local Run button. Other participants see output attributed to that device and source revision. Sharing sends source to the relay; the [MCP guide](/guide/mcp) explains capabilities, expiry and how Claude or Codex can help edit without automatically executing code.

Ask an assistant to propose a calendar test case, predict both Add and AddDate results, and explain which requirement each operation satisfies. Review the source and press Run yourself. Keep this as an experiment in semantics: a passing demonstration does not turn NextDay into a complete recurring-job scheduler or prove a particular host's wall-clock behavior under every operational condition.

sections.title: Keep the time contract beside the feature
sections.body:
A useful review records the kind of time involved, location rules, accepted representation, precision, timeout ownership, recurrence policy and test cases. It also explains what happens when the process restarts, rules change, a deadline expires or delivery is retried. Those decisions make the code reviewable beyond its use of a familiar time API.

For the document service, the thirty-second conversion budget stays an elapsed-work constraint. The local morning digest keeps a location-aware recurrence policy and separately tracked occurrences. The editorial date remains a date label. Each feature can now choose its implementation and tests without pretending that all time values have the same meaning.

Continue with the [time-and-units lesson](/learn/clean-production.time-money), [timer ownership](/learn/stdlib.timer-contracts), and [I/O boundaries](/news/go-streaming-io-reader-eof-limits-json). The value of the model is practical: an unexpected timestamp stops being a mysterious formatting bug once the team can identify which contract was crossed and which evidence would demonstrate the intended behavior.

title: Go concurrency: mutexes, invariants and atomic snapshots
description: Understand lost updates despite synchronized access, protect complete transitions and publish immutable snapshots. Tested Go code and hands-on Playground exercises.

sections.title: Start with the rule the state must preserve
sections.body:
A service passes its race-detector tests, yet occasionally loses an increment, oversells a limited work slot, or publishes mismatched configuration fields. The first instinct is often to add another lock or replace a map with sync.Map. Before choosing a primitive, write down the invariant: the relationship that must remain true after every accepted operation.

For a counter, two accepted increments should produce an increase of two. For a reservation, accepted units must not exceed available units. For a configuration snapshot, a version and its associated limits should belong to the same publication. These are application rules. A synchronization primitive helps implement them, but it cannot infer which separate method calls the application intended to treat as one operation.

This guide uses an original standard-library lab to separate memory safety, operation atomicity and ownership. Its controlled lost-update example deliberately uses synchronized accesses throughout. We checked the correct implementation and its demonstrations with native Go 1.27.3, repeated tests and the race detector. There are no timing-based benchmark claims: the point is a reproducible semantic failure and a testable repair.

sections.title: A race-free read and write can still lose an update
sections.body:
The lab's Counter has Load and Store methods, each protected by the same mutex. Two goroutines call Load, calculate the next value, then call Store. A channel barrier guarantees that both loads observe zero before either store begins. Both goroutines therefore store one, and the final count is one.

| Controlled step | Goroutine A | Goroutine B | Stored value |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Initial state | Waiting | Waiting | 0 |
| Read separately | Reads 0 | Reads 0 | 0 |
| Calculate locally | Computes 1 | Computes 1 | 0 |
| Store separately | Stores 1 | Stores 1 | 1 |

Every access to the shared integer is locked. The failure is the gap between the protected operations, not a broken mutex. The [Go memory model](https://go.dev/ref/mem) describes synchronization relationships; our application still needs to choose the operation those relationships protect.

The fixture is deterministic because it coordinates the reads explicitly. It does not increase loop counts until a failure happens or insert sleeps in the hope of making the scheduler cooperate. A single run explains the result. That makes the example useful in code review: a reviewer can point to the exact interval in which another operation invalidates the caller's assumption.

sections.title: Protect the complete transition
Use the race detector for the question it can answer
sections.body:
The [race-detector guide](https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector) explains that detection depends on executed code paths. A clean run is useful evidence about those paths. It is not proof that every possible workload is race-free, and it is not a proof of business correctness.

Our lost-update fixture should continue to return one while remaining free of unsynchronized memory accesses. Treating that fixture's successful execution as an application success would miss its purpose. The test names distinguish the deliberately incorrect composition from the complete Add operation that must preserve all increments.

Use different assertions for different questions. Race detection checks memory-access behavior. A reservation test checks accepted capacity. A snapshot test checks whether fields come from one version. An ownership test changes a returned map and checks that internal state did not change. A lifecycle test checks that workers have finished when their owner returns.

Run those checks together, but keep their claims separate in the review. A team that says only all tests passed may accidentally omit the invariant that motivated the change. A stronger report names the accepted transition, the competing callers and the outcome that would demonstrate a defect. The [concurrency-testing guide](/news/go-concurrency-tests-synctest-without-sleeps) shows how explicit coordination helps make those assertions reliable.

sections.title: Decide which state belongs under one owner
sections.body:
A cache entry may contain a value, an expiry and an accounting charge. A registry may contain a membership map and a count. Protecting the map while updating the related count under an unrelated lock can expose states that the feature never intended to publish. Start with the relationship, then choose the ownership boundary.

The older [Go maps article](https://go.dev/blog/maps) explains why ordinary maps need appropriate coordination for concurrent access. A lock around the map addresses that access requirement. It does not automatically protect a separate counter, a pointer stored inside a value, or a larger operation that spans several lookups.

Draw the state as a small ownership graph. Which fields change together? Which values can callers retain? Which operation may create or remove an entry? What result should a concurrent reader observe if it arrives between two modifications? Those questions often reveal that a convenient generic Store method is exposing too much of the implementation.

Prefer methods named after useful operations when they clarify the invariant: Reserve, ReplaceConfiguration, CompleteJob or RemoveAndReturn. Avoid promising atomicity for a workflow merely because each helper is individually synchronized. The companion [retry and idempotency guide](/news/go-retries-idempotency-keys-unknown-outcomes) applies the same reasoning to a recorded effect and the receipt used to recognize its retry.

sections.title: Choose mutex, RWMutex and sync.Map from the workload
sections.body:
A plain mutex is often the simplest way to keep a compound transition understandable. An RWMutex may help a suitable read-heavy workload, but it changes the locking discipline and should be justified with representative measurements. Counting reader methods is not enough to establish that read-lock coordination will improve an actual service.

The [sync package reference](https://pkg.go.dev/sync) describes sync.Map as a specialized type and identifies its intended workloads. A concurrent map is not a general transaction across multiple entries and external state. A Load followed by a Store still expresses two operations unless the chosen API provides the complete conditional transition you need.

Similarly, LoadOrStore does not automatically make an expensive preparation step outside the call execute once. Several callers can prepare candidate values before one candidate becomes the stored value. If preparation acquires resources or triggers effects, give that work its own ownership and duplicate-suppression policy. Storing one winning value does not undo the losing preparations.

Choose the simplest primitive that enforces the required transition, then measure contention if it matters. This lab does not rank synchronization types by speed. Its evidence concerns values, ownership and controlled interleavings. The [lock-ownership lesson](/learn/concurrency.lock-ownership) connects those decisions to copy rules and pointer receivers.

sections.title: Atomic publication does not freeze the published object
sections.body:
An atomic pointer can publish a completed configuration so readers observe one selected pointer value. The [atomic package](https://pkg.go.dev/sync/atomic) defines its synchronization semantics. Those semantics do not make later ordinary mutations of the pointed-to map safe, and they do not turn several unrelated loads into one application snapshot.

Our ConfigStore constructs a fresh configuration and never modifies that published version afterward. Writers serialize the read-copy-patch-publish sequence with a mutex, preventing two writers from silently replacing each other's patches. Publication uses an atomic pointer; writer coordination remains explicit.

```go
s.writers.Lock()
defer s.writers.Unlock()
next := clone(old.rates)
for key, value := range patch {
    next[key] = value
}
s.active.Store(&config{rates: next})
```

This is an excerpt; the downloadable implementation also handles the initial empty state. The patch map must remain unchanged by its caller during the call. After the operation returns, callers may change their own inputs without mutating the published configuration because the store owns separate map storage.

The design is not presented as a universal lock-free optimization. It still copies data and allocates, and the runtime has its own costs. Readers do not acquire the writer mutex in this implementation, but a performance claim would require measuring the actual read and update workload.

sections.title: A snapshot must preserve one version and its ownership
Keep blocking work outside a local state transition deliberately
sections.body:
Holding a mutex while waiting for a slow dependency can extend contention and make cancellation or shutdown harder to reason about. Simply unlocking before the dependency call, however, may reopen the exact invariant gap the mutex was intended to close. The solution is to model the intermediate state rather than pretend the whole workflow disappeared.

A job manager might reserve a slot under the lock, release the lock while doing external work, then finalize that specific reservation under the lock. It needs an operation identifier, a cancellation path and a rule for releasing abandoned capacity. Another caller must not mistake reserved-but-unfinished work for available capacity or a completed result.

If the process can restart, local mutex ownership is not enough to recover that intermediate state. Persisted workflows and external effects require additional records and reconciliation. The local critical section and the distributed operation are different boundaries, even when the function that coordinates them has one convenient name.

The [bounded-work article](/news/go-backpressure-concurrency-limits-queues-deadlines) covers admission and waiting budgets. Combine those limits with a clear state machine: admitted, reserved, completed, rejected or uncertain. This makes it possible to decide what a timeout changes and what another participant is allowed to retry.

sections.title: Channels can express ownership, but they do not copy it for you
sections.body:
A single goroutine processing commands can own a map and its related counters. That can make a complex transition easier to serialize. Send the complete intended command, not a read request followed later by a separate write that assumes the answer is still current. The operation boundary still matters even when there is no shared-map lock in the caller.

Sending a slice or map through a channel also does not automatically create independent backing storage. Decide whether the sender transfers ownership, shares immutable data, or retains a mutable copy. A channel provides communication; the API must provide the lifetime and mutation contract.

Bound the command queue and define what happens when the owner stops. A caller waiting forever for a reply is not a successful ownership design merely because all map accesses occur in one goroutine. Cancellation, rejection and joining need explicit paths.

Use the [mutex-or-handoff lesson](/learn/concurrency.mutex) and [cancel-and-join lesson](/learn/concurrency.cancel-and-join) together. They help distinguish state protection from lifecycle completion. A worker that has received a cancellation signal may still be using its state, so cleanup should follow evidence of completion rather than the existence of a signal alone.

sections.title: Preserve the synchronization object's identity
sections.body:
Types containing active mutexes or atomic state should not be casually copied after use. Pointer receivers and constructors returning pointers help make the intended identity visible, but callers and helper functions still need to respect it. A value copy can separate the lock from the state relationships the original object was supposed to protect.

Run go vet as part of the review and inspect copy-lock diagnostics when they appear. The [vet command reference](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/vet) describes its role as a checker for suspicious constructs. Static checks complement tests; they do not replace a review of the actual ownership contract.

Avoid returning internal map storage just to make a getter cheap. If copying snapshots is too expensive for a measured workload, choose another explicit interface, such as a read-only operation over one internally retained version. Consider how that interface prevents references from escaping and whether callbacks can block or reenter the owner.

A useful optimization preserves the invariant while changing its cost. Removing ownership boundaries to improve a microbenchmark changes the API's behavior, not just its implementation. The [allocation-profiling guide](/news/go-allocation-profiling-pprof-escape-benchmarks) shows how to separate measured resource improvements from changes to the output contract.

sections.title: Explore the interleaving in Playground
sections.body:
[Download the synchronization and retry lab](/downloads/go-reliability-lab-20261029.zip). The invariants/main.go program is self-contained and uses standard-library packages. Before replacing an existing [Playground](/playground) draft, download your source copy. Paste the program into main.go and keep a compatible go.mod. The browser editor does not execute Go or automatically create a room.

Predict the controlled lost-update result before running. Replace the composed Load and Store calls with one complete Add and compare the result. Change the reservation request to exactly the remaining capacity, then one unit above it. Mutate the returned snapshot and check whether a later snapshot changes. Each mutation should test one named contract.

If you choose to collaborate, create a temporary room, open it in a compatible GopherForge native app and press Run on the device where the code should execute. Other participants receive output attributed to that device and source revision. The [MCP guide](/guide/mcp) explains link roles, expiry and how Claude or Codex can help edit. AI edits do not automatically run the program.

The complete suite adds repeated concurrent callers, coherent snapshot checks and deliberately broken negative variants. Run go test -race -count=50 ./... and go vet ./... from the downloaded module. The standalone programs also cross-compile for wasip1/wasm; that build check is separate from certifying every host's runtime behavior. The goal is a clear invariant, a controlled competing operation and evidence that the implementation preserves the rule the feature actually needs.

title: Go retries: idempotency keys and unknown outcomes
description: Design retry-safe Go operations with stable keys, matching inputs, recorded receipts and explicit unknown outcomes. Includes a tested lab and Playground exercises.

sections.title: A timeout describes the caller's observation
sections.body:
A document-conversion request reaches a service, reserves seven processing units and commits a result. The response disappears before the client receives it. The client sees a timeout or connection error. Did the work fail? From that observation alone, the client may not know. Repeating the operation with a fresh identity can apply the effect again even though the first attempt completed successfully.

This guide separates retry policy from duplicate-effect prevention. A retry decides whether and when to make another attempt. An idempotency contract decides which attempts represent the same logical operation and how the service recognizes their outcome. Backoff can reduce pressure, but it cannot recognize an already committed operation by itself.

The downloadable Go lab makes the lost-response window explicit without a real network. One function commits an in-memory effect and receipt, then deliberately drops the returned reply. The next call uses the same key. The example is original, bounded and reproducible; it is not a durable database, a payment integration or a universal exactly-once execution mechanism.

sections.title: Distinguish failure before work from an unknown outcome
sections.body:
Different failure points require different decisions. A rejected input may never enter the business operation. A client may abandon a call while the service continues. A database commit may succeed while the reply is lost. A remote dependency may perform its effect before the local service manages to record that fact.

| Evidence available | What can be concluded | Useful next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definitive validation rejection before admission | This operation was not accepted | Correct the input |
| Caller deadline elapsed | Caller stopped waiting | Preserve identity; inspect the operation contract |
| Stored committed receipt for the same key | The recorded operation completed | Return or reconcile that result |
| External effect with missing local record | Local evidence is incomplete | Reconcile with the external owner |

The [HTTP semantics specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2) defines method idempotency, but an application still needs to understand its actual operation. A response status or a transport exception is not a complete transaction log. Do not infer that no business effect occurred merely because the client did not receive a successful response.

In particular, unknown is often the caller's knowledge state, not a special row that every service stores. The lab's service knows it committed; its simulated caller has lost the response. Keeping those viewpoints separate makes reconciliation much easier to explain.

sections.title: Give the logical operation a stable identity
sections.body:
The client should preserve the same operation key across attempts that are intended to represent one action. Generating a new key after every timeout declares a different operation to a service whose contract uses that key for deduplication. The second request may then be entirely valid and still produce the duplicate effect the client wanted to avoid.

Our toy request contains a job name and a positive unit count. The store compares those typed fields when a key already exists. A matching request receives the original receipt identifier and committed total, with separate replay metadata. A valid but different job name or unit count produces a conflict and does not change state.

```go
if old, ok := s.records[key]; ok {
    if old.request != req {
        return Receipt{}, ErrConflict
    }
    replay := old.receipt
    replay.Replayed = true
    return replay, nil
}
```

Choose the identity scope deliberately in a real API. An operation name, API version and authorized caller scope may be part of the contract. An idempotency key is not authentication or permission to retrieve somebody else's result. Avoid putting secrets or personal information into keys just to make them recognizable in logs.

The [Stripe idempotency documentation](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) is a concrete provider example and distinguishes API-version behavior. Read the selected provider's actual replay, conflict and retention rules instead of assuming that every API implements this lab's contract.

sections.title: Record the effect and receipt under one boundary
sections.body:
If the business effect can commit without the deduplication record, a retry may see no record and apply the effect again. If a completed-looking receipt can be stored before the effect is actually committed, a retry may incorrectly report success. The relationship between those two records is the core invariant.

In the lab, one mutex protects the total, lookup and receipt insertion. Both the effect and its receipt exist in the same process memory and are changed within one local critical section. This makes the example's concurrency behavior easy to test, while leaving durability explicitly outside its claim.

```go
s.total += req.Units
res := Receipt{ID: len(s.records) + 1, Total: s.total}
s.records[key] = record{request: req, receipt: res}
return res, nil
```

For a database-backed service, put the relevant local business change and idempotency result inside an appropriate database transaction. The [Go transaction guide](https://go.dev/doc/database/execute-transactions) explains using a transaction object for the operations that belong to it. Mixing unrelated pool calls into the workflow can accidentally move work outside the intended transaction.
